When he says: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, Allah says: My servant has glorified Me. When he says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, Allah says: This is between Me and My servant in halves, and for My servant is what he asks. When he says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, Allah says: This is for My servant, and for My servant is what he asks."

You will find in the mushaf that it is counted among its verses, as verse (1), but this is based on a weak opinion, and the correct view is that its verses are seven: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾, ﴿not of those who have evoked anger or of those who are astray﴾ — seven verses.

Allah, mighty and majestic, says: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿By those that scatter with dispersal (1), and those that carry the heavy load (2), and those that glide with ease (3), and those that distribute by command (4)﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 1–4]. Allah the Exalted swore by these creatures because they indicate His greatness, blessed and exalted, and because of the benefits and interests they contain.

As for His saying ﴿By those that scatter﴾: adh-dhariyat are the winds that scatter dust and other than dust. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿So it becomes dry debris which the winds scatter﴾ [Al-Kahf 45]. ﴿Becomes dry debris which the winds scatter﴾ means: disperses it in many places.

Allah swore by the scattering winds because of their many benefits; in their variation there is profound wisdom. Among them are warm winds and among them are cold winds, according to what the wisdom of Allah, mighty and majestic, requires. Also, the winds stir up clouds, and by them Allah waters the earth; and because they move ships. In earlier times ships sailed by the winds. Allah said: ﴿Until, when you are in the ships and they sail with them by a favorable wind and they rejoice in it, there comes a violent wind and the waves come to them from everywhere﴾ [Yunus 22].

As for His saying ﴿those that carry the heavy load﴾: it refers to the clouds, which carry water laden, i.e., heavy and burdened. They are heavy, laden with great waters, seas; therefore the earth is rained upon and you find rivers on the earth by the permission of Allah, mighty and majestic.

So: adh-dhariyat are the winds, al-hamilat are the clouds, and the connection between them is clear, because the winds are what stir up the clouds, and also what fertilize the clouds with water. Allah said: ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing, then We sent down water from the sky and gave you drink from it﴾ [Al-Hijr 22].

Allah said: ﴿those that glide with ease﴾. ﴿Al-jariyat﴾ are the ships; ﴿with ease﴾ means easily. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ [Al-Haqqah 11], i.e., in the ship. These ships glide, made easy by the permission of Allah, mighty and majestic, by the good winds that Allah has made easy.

﴿Al-jariyat yusra﴾ are the ships, gliding by the permission of Allah, mighty and majestic, made easy and facilitated; and whenever the wind is suitable, their movement is easier.

Now there are ships powered by engines that do not need the winds, so they have become easier and easier; you see them as complete villages cutting through the waves, moving with ease.

The connection between these three: the clouds carry rains which fall to the earth, and in them is provision for livestock and people.

﴿Al-jariyat﴾ means the ships; they also carry provisions from one place to another. It is not possible for provisions to reach another land with a sea between them except by means of ships.

﴿Amran﴾ means those who distribute the affair, i.e., the affairs of creation. It may also mean "by the command of Allah," and the meaning is correct in both interpretations; for these angels, upon them be peace, distribute what Allah wills of the provision of creatures and other things by the command of Allah, mighty and majestic. Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 51, verse 7–9:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By the sky, full of paths﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 7]. "The sky" is well known. "Dhat" means "possessor of." "Al-hubuk" means "the paths," meaning that, because of its beauty, it is as if it possesses well-woven, precisely formed paths, just as you see in sand dunes: you find them with ridges, and the wind, despite its abundance over them, leaves them with ridges. So the sky is likewise, ﴿full of paths﴾.

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, you are in a contradictory saying﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 8]. "Indeed you" is addressed to the disbelievers. "In a contradictory saying" means that some of it contradicts other parts. How is that? Some of the disbelievers said to the Messenger (ﷺ): "He is a madman." That is one saying. Some of them said: "He is a sorcerer." That is one saying. Some said: "He is a soothsayer." That is one saying. Some said: "He is a poet." That is one saying. Some said: "He is a liar." That is one saying. So they disagree about the Prophet (ﷺ), and the disagreement of their sayings shows their falsehood and corruption. Whenever you see a saying that is contradictory and self-conflicting, know that it is false and not sound, because the truth cannot be self-contradictory. These deniers of the Messenger (ﷺ) have disagreed, as you have heard.

﴿Indeed, you are in a contradictory saying (8). Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 8, 9]. "Yu'fak" means "is turned away." Regarding "ʿanhu" (from it), it has been said: the pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning that whoever is turned away from among the people is turned away from the Messenger (ﷺ).

It has also been said: the pronoun refers to the saying, and according to this view "ʿan" carries the meaning of "bi" (with), meaning: by this saying, whoever is turned away is turned away, and by this saying one is turned away from the truth. These two meanings are mutually connected, and the closer view is that the pronoun in His words ﴿from it﴾ refers to the saying, because it is the nearest thing mentioned.

﴿Indeed, you are in a contradictory saying (8). Turned away from it﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 8, 9], i.e., from this saying, i.e., because of it, ﴿whoever is turned away﴾, i.e., whoever is turned away from the truth. This is because there is a kind of sorcery in eloquence: when an eloquent, articulate man comes to you and begins presenting doubts and suspicions to you, are you not deceived by his words? Yes.

These deniers of the Messenger (ﷺ) have eloquence, have rhetoric, have deception and trickery, and so they turn people away. As for His words, ﴿whoever is turned away﴾: is the meaning whoever Allah has decreed should be turned away? Or is the meaning ﴿whoever is turned away﴾, i.e., whoever these contradictory people have turned away? The two are also mutually connected, for these who lead people astray cannot lead them astray except by the permission of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: "Whom Allah leads astray, there is no guide for him, and whom He guides, there is no misleader for him." They are the ones who turn people away, i.e., they turn them away as a cause; they are the cause, but the one who decrees the turning away is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

But know, my Muslim brother, that no one can be turned away from the truth except someone whom Allah knows to be unworthy of the truth. We ask Allah for safety for us and for you. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 124]. Likewise, ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ refers to those who comply with it and believe in it. What we have said is indicated by the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [as-Saff 5]. But beware, when you see someone astray, of saying: "This one is not worthy of guidance," because there is a difference between speaking in generality and speaking in specificity.

Speaking in specificity is forbidden, because you may see a person astray, think "this one will not be guided," and then Allah guides him, blessed and exalted is He. And the reverse is also true: you may see a person upright and say, "This one cannot go astray," and then Allah leads him astray. The main point is: beware of testifying for a specific person. But in reality, when you see someone astray, rebellious, arrogant toward the truth, you may in your heart consider it unlikely that Allah will guide him; yet do not say that Allah will not guide him. Has it not reached you that a man was diligent in worship, and there was another who was extravagant toward himself, and this worshipper would pass by him and advise him, but the other would say: "You cannot come between me and my Lord; leave me and my Lord." One day the diligent worshipper said: "By Allah, Allah will not forgive you," or he said: "By Allah, Allah will not admit you into Paradise." Then Allah, exalted is He, said: "Who is it that swears by Me that I will not forgive so-and-so? I have forgiven him and nullified your deeds." [Related by Muslim (2621/137) from the hadith of Jundub ibn 'Abdullah al-Bajali.] We ask Allah for well-being. Therefore do not be conceited about yourself, and do not despair of the mercy of Allah, neither regarding yourself nor regarding others, for Allah is powerful over all things.

But we know, in a general sense, that if a person is not worthy of guidance, he will not be guided. So when we see this person deviant, arrogant, and obstinate, there is no doubt that it prevails in our assessment that he is not worthy of guidance; yet it is not for us to say so. It is forbidden for us to utter it, and it is feared that it may be said to us as it was said to that man: "I have forgiven him and nullified your deeds."

Here is an important point: the difference between specification and generalization. For example, we testify for every believer that he is in Paradise. But if we see an upright person who prays, gives zakat, fasts, performs Hajj, gives charity, does good, honors his parents and maintains ties of kinship, do we testify that he is in Paradise? No.

Specification is one thing, and generalization is another. If we see a disbelieving, atheistic man empowered over the Muslims, tearing up the Book of Allah and trampling it with his feet, and mocking Allah and His Messenger, do we say: "This one is among the people of the Fire"? No. Rather we say: "Whoever does this is among the people of the Fire," and we do not specify an individual, because it is possible, at the last moment, that Allah bestows His favor on him and guides him; you do not know. Therefore you must distinguish between specification and generalization, or between specification and generalization in general terms.

A man died, and we know that he died as a Christian according to what appears to us from his condition. Do we testify that he is in the Fire? We do not testify, because first, if he is among the people of the Fire, he will enter it even if we do not testify; and if he is not among the people of the Fire, then our testimony is testimony without knowledge. Such matters have no need for this. For instance, if someone said: "A man of the Russians, one of the atheists among them, died; a man of the Americans, one of the atheists, died; a Jew, one of the atheists," curse him and testify that he is in the Fire, we would say: that is not possible. We say: whoever dies upon this, he is among the people of the Fire; whoever dies upon this, we curse him. But a specific individual, no. For this reason it has been part of the creed of Ahl as-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah that they said: we do not testify for anyone that he is in Paradise or in the Fire, except for those for whom the Prophet (ﷺ) testified. Yet we hope for good for the doer of good, and we fear for the evildoer. This is the creed of Ahl as-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah.

However, the correct view is that qatala means "destroyed," because there is no need to turn it away from its apparent meaning, and its apparent meaning is sound and straightforward. So the meaning of ﴿qutila﴾ is: "destroyed."

And ﴿al-kharrasun﴾ is the plural of kharras (conjecturer), who is one who speaks by guesswork, conjecture, doubt and suspicion, because he is immersed in ignorance, heedlessness and negligence. For this reason He described them by His saying: ﴿who are in a heedless flood, forgetful﴾, meaning: in a flood of ignorance that has surrounded them from every side. ﴿Forgetful﴾ means heedless, not seeking to accept what Allah sent down to His messengers, upon them be prayers and peace.

Among their ignorance is that they ﴿ask: When is the Day of Recompense?﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 12], asking in a manner of denial and disbelief. Had they been asking in a manner of seeking knowledge and information, they would have been excused, just as Jibril said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Tell me about the Hour." But did he say it in denial and disbelief? No, rather as a question seeking information. The Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him and his family, said: "The one asked about it is no more knowledgeable than the one asking" [narrated by Muslim (8/1) from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab].

But those conjecturers ﴿ask: When is the Day of Recompense?﴾ — meaning: when is it? — in disbelief. For this reason Allah said of them in Surah Qaf: ﴿So the disbelievers said: This is a strange thing. When we have died and become dust, that is a far-off return﴾ [Qaf 2-3], meaning: Will we return after we were dust? That is a far-off return.

So they ask about the Day of Resurrection not as a question of inquiry and information seeking certainty, but as a question of denial and disbelief.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 13]. This is the answer, meaning the Day of Resurrection: ﴿The Day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾. On this basis, ﴿yawm﴾ here is an adverbial complement, the predicate of an omitted subject, and the implied sense is: the Day of Resurrection is ﴿the Day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾.

The meaning of ﴿tormented over the Fire﴾ is: they will be presented to it and burned by it, because fitnah here means burning; but it is followed by ﴿ʿala﴾ because it is given the meaning of "presented." That is, they will be presented to the Fire and burned in it. This is the Day of Recompense.

﴿The Day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾ ﴿Taste your trial; this is what you used to seek to hasten﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 13-14]. ﴿Taste﴾ is a sentence in the position of a speech, following an omitted saying. The implied sense: it will be said to them: ﴿Taste your trial﴾.

﴿Taste your trial﴾ is a command of humiliation and degradation, meaning: taste your burning in the Fire which you used to deny.

﴿This is what you used to seek to hasten﴾, because they used to say: ﴿When is this promise, if you are truthful?﴾ [Yunus 48], seeking to hasten the Hour in mockery of it. As Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it, while those who believe are apprehensive of it and know that it is the truth﴾ [ash-Shura 18]. So it is said to these: ﴿Taste your trial; this is what you used to seek to hasten﴾, and it is said to them: ﴿Is this magic, or do you not see? Burn in it, and be patient or be not patient; it is the same for you. You are only recompensed for what you used to do﴾ [at-Tur 15-16].

Now I ask you: they are tormented over the Fire and burned by it, and it is said: ﴿Taste your trial.﴾ What do you understand from this? Do you understand that in this there is physical and psychological punishment? Yes, because burning is physical punishment; whenever their skins are roasted, they are given other skins in their place.

﴿Taste your trial; this is what you used to seek to hasten﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 14] is a rebuke, humiliation and degradation. What punishment does this involve? Psychological punishment. Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 51, verse 15:

When he mentioned the punishment of these deniers who speculate, He said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 15]. ﴿Al-muttaqin﴾ (the righteous) are those who have feared Allah. You see that taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) occurs in the Noble Qur'an in many aspects: sometimes as a description, sometimes as a verb, sometimes as a command, and sometimes it is attributed to Allah, and sometimes attributed to punishment, and other than that. The point is that this indicates that taqwa is of great importance in Islam, and taqwa is not merely a statement uttered by the tongue; rather, it is a statement followed by action and implementation.

If you ask: What is taqwa? We say: taqwa consists of two things: doing what Allah has commanded, and abstaining from what Allah has forbidden. This is taqwa: doing what He commanded and avoiding what He forbade, with knowledge, certainty, seeking reward, and fear. You do what Allah has commanded because you know that Allah commanded it; you do what Allah has commanded because you seek its reward: the good deed is rewarded tenfold up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples.

You abstain from what Allah has forbidden because you know that Allah forbade it; you abstain from what Allah has forbidden out of fear of Allah's punishment, because you are certain of the torment. This is taqwa.

﴿Al-muttaqin﴾ — He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿in gardens and springs﴾, meaning: they will be settled in gardens and springs. The word "jannat" is the plural of "jannah" (garden). You encounter in the Qur'an "jannah" in the singular and "jannat" in the plural. Are they many gardens or one garden? They are many gardens, but it is mentioned in the singular form as a matter of naming the category; otherwise they are gardens. Look at the end of Surah ar-Rahman: Allah mentions four gardens. He said: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [ar-Rahman 46], then He said: ﴿And besides them are two gardens﴾ [ar-Rahman 62]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Two gardens of gold, their vessels and what is in them, and two gardens of silver, their vessels and what is in them." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4878) and Muslim (180 / 296) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.] So the gardens are indeed many.

﴿Ākhidhīna mā ātāhum rabbuhum﴾ [adh-Dhāriyāt: 16]. His saying, ﴿ākhidhīna﴾, is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the implicit pronoun in the predicate, meaning: while they are ﴿taking what their Lord has given them﴾, i.e., what He has bestowed upon them of delight. This verse is like the verse in Surat at-Ṭūr: ﴿fākihīna bimā ātāhum rabbuhum﴾ [aṭ-Ṭūr: 18], meaning: what Allah has bestowed upon them of delight in these Gardens. Then He explained the cause by which they attained this, saying: ﴿Innahum kānū qabla dhālika muḥsinīn﴾ (Indeed, they were, before that, doers of good).

﴿Kānū qabla dhālika﴾ means: in the worldly life, ﴿muḥsinīn﴾, i.e., standing in obedience to Allah in the manner that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is pleased with. It has been authentically related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Ihsān is that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] This is ihsān in worship. As for ihsān in dealing with creation, the most comprehensive thing said about it is what the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever wishes to be distanced from the Fire and admitted into Paradise, let his death come while he believes in Allah and the Last Day, and let him treat people with what he would like to be treated with."[[Narrated by Muslim (1844/46) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr.]] This is ihsān toward people: that you treat people with what you love to be treated with, from good character, cheerful countenance, restraining harm, and giving generously, and other things that are well known. Thus, these are the doers of good in the worship of Allah, and doers of good to the servants of Allah. ﴿Kānū qabla dhālika﴾ means: before they took what Allah had bestowed upon them of delight, they were doers of good.

Then he elaborated on this goodness, or elaborated on a kind of this goodness, saying: ﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 17]. The word ﴿مَا﴾ (ma) here is said to be superfluous in wording, but not superfluous in meaning, and the intended construction is: ﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾, i.e., they slept little. And what did they do in this wakefulness? They did what Allah mentioned in Surat al-Muzzammil: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it, and [so do] a group of those with you﴾ [al-Muzzammil 20].

They were not staying up for amusement, idle talk, or waking to such things; rather, their sleep was little so that they could devote themselves to obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 51, verse 18:

﴿They used to sleep but little of the night, and at the dawn they would seek forgiveness﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 17, 18]

﴿Al-asḥar﴾ is the plural of saḥar (the last part of the night), and ﴿they seek forgiveness﴾ means they ask Allah for forgiveness. This is from the goodness of their deeds and their not being pleased with themselves, and from their awareness that, however much they strive, they fall short. So they seek Allah's forgiveness after performing an act of obedience, to make up for whatever defect occurred in it. You know that it is prescribed at the end of acts of worship that a person ask his Lord for forgiveness for whatever shortcoming may have occurred in them. Thus, after the prayer, a person asks his Lord for forgiveness three times. And after Hajj, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and remember Him as He has guided you, though before that you were among those who were astray. Then depart from where the people depart, and ask Allah for forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198, 199].

So they ask for forgiveness after their tahajjud (night prayer), their standing in prayer, and their staying awake in obedience to Allah, out of fear that there may have been some shortcoming. This indicates their knowledge of themselves and that they regard themselves as falling short, unlike what some people do today: when such a person worships Allah with even the least act of worship, he becomes arrogant with himself, boasts about it before Allah the Exalted, and thinks that he is among the righteous servants of Allah.

It is true that a person should hope, when Allah grants him the ability to obey Him, that Allah will accept it. But if he regards himself as having completed everything, then it is feared for that person that his deeds will be nullified while he is unaware.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 51, verse 19:

﴿And in the nights before dawn they would seek forgiveness (18). And in their wealth there was a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 18, 19] In all their wealth; whether it is zakatable wealth or non-zakatable wealth, there is a right in it ﴿for the beggar and the deprived﴾. When a beggar comes to them, they give him; when they see one who is deprived, meaning one who is prevented from provision and is poor, they give him. Their wealth has been set aside for what pleases Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, such as giving to the beggar and the deprived and other lawful spending. Thus they are engaged in obedience to Allah: night prayer, seeking forgiveness, and spending of wealth; but without extravagance (israf) and without arrogance (makhilah).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 51, verse 20:**

﴿And in their wealth there was a right for the beggar and the deprived (19). And on the earth are signs for those who have certainty.﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 19, 20].

﴿On the earth are signs for those who have certainty.﴾ Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not specify these signs. Rather, the word is indefinite so that it encompasses every sign on the earth, whether they are the events that occur upon it or are found in the very nature and composition of the earth, for in it are great signs.

﴿On the earth are signs﴾ in terms of its composition, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And on the earth are neighboring tracts﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4]. You find a single rock containing several minerals, though it is one rock. Sometimes you see in the mountains ﴿white and red streaks of varying shades, and jet-black ones﴾ [Fatir: 27].

You also find on it soft, crumbly land and hard land, and other great signs known to the scholars of geology. There are signs in terms of the events that occur on it: earthquakes, volcanoes, and others.

There are also signs in terms of the nature of the atmosphere: heat and cold, violent winds, cold winds, and warm winds, and other things which, when a person reflects on them, he recognizes the power of Allah, Exalted, on one hand, and recognizes His wisdom and mercy on the other hand. For the signs of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, are contemplated by a person not only in terms of power and greatness, but even in terms of wisdom and mercy, because you find everything suited to its place and time, and everything you find is among the effects of the mercy of Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

The important point is that the word ﴿signs﴾ is, as we find, a general indefinite term for everything that occurs on the earth of signs, and for everything in it of its nature, composition, and other things.

﴿Signs for those who have certainty﴾ meaning: for the one who has certainty of the existence of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His greatness and majesty. As for the one who doubts, may Allah protect us, he will not benefit from these signs; rather, these signs may become a harm to him. The cosmic signs and the legislated signs may be good for a person and may be evil. Listen to the words of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, some of them say, "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?" As for those who believe, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. But as for those in whose hearts is disease, it has added to their impurity the impurity [of their own], and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawba: 124, 125].

Likewise with the cosmic signs: among people are those who benefit from them and derive from them evidence of the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and among people are those who, on the contrary, what they find of signs leads them to atheism, may Allah protect us. For this reason He said: ﴿On the earth are signs for those who have certainty﴾, meaning: not for everyone, but for the one with certainty. As for the doubter, the wavering one, and the disbeliever, he will not benefit from these signs.

And [within] yourselves too there are signs; will you not then see? The word "signs" (āyāt) is omitted here. For this reason, in its grammatical analysis (i'rab), the phrase ﴿in yourselves﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as the predicate of an omitted subject, and the full sense is: "And in yourselves are signs." The wisdom behind this, Allah knows best, and in our limited knowledge we think, is that Allah omitted these signs because they are closer to a person and more intimately connected to him than the earth is, since they lie within himself: "in yourselves are signs."

The signs within the self are not only in the composition of the body, nor only in the faculties Allah has placed in it, but also in the changes of states. You find a person shifting from joy to sorrow and from grief to happiness, wondrous and great transformations. A person may find himself changed in a single moment, and sometimes he finds himself changed without any cause. He may be open-hearted, spacious in mind, and joyful, and then suddenly he becomes constricted and sorrowful without a reason, and sometimes the reverse. This applies to psychological states.

Likewise, it applies to states of faith, which are greater and more consequential. You find a person at times possessing such certainty that it is as if he witnesses the unseen with his senses, as if he sees the Throne, as if he sees the heavens, as if he sees the angels, as if he sees everything Allah has informed us of concerning the unseen. At other times this certainty diminishes, for reasons that may be known or unknown. Among the known reasons is little obedience, for little obedience is one of the causes of weakened certainty. When a person's obedience decreases, his certainty weakens. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But if they turn away, then know that Allah intends only to afflict them for some of their sins﴾ [al-Ma'idah 49].

There are also causes that a person does not know. Among them are frivolity and heedlessness. For this reason, the Companions said to the Messenger (ﷺ): "When we are with you and you mention Paradise and the Fire, it is as if we see them with our own eyes; but when we go back to our families and attend to our children and wives, or as they said, we forget." [Recorded by Muslim (2750/12) from the hadith of Handhalah al-Asadi.] Thus, whenever a person is distracted by amusements, his certainty and faith decrease. For this reason the Sharia forbade games and vain amusement, through which a person grows further from obedience to Allah and from reflection upon the signs of Allah.

Also within the self are signs in the souls of people. Some people you find gentle, easygoing, open-faced, and joyful; everyone who sees them is pleased by their countenance, and everyone who sits with them has his grief and worry lifted. Other people are the opposite: frowning and stern the moment you see them, so that if you were joyful, sorrow and ill feeling would come upon you. This too is among the signs of the self, and they are very numerous. Whoever wishes more on this, and to appreciate the power of Allah the Exalted in the signs within ourselves, should consult the words of Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, in Miftah Dar al-Sa'adah, and he will find marvels upon marvels. Likewise, in his small book, which is great in meaning, al-Tibyan fi Aqsam al-Quran, he mentions many such wonders.

﴿Will you not then see?﴾ The interrogative here is for rebuke and denial, as if Allah the Mighty and Majestic were saying: "Look within yourselves, reflect, ponder, and contemplate." If you do not recognize these signs, then you are not seeing. So the question here is for rebuke and denial: "Will you not then reflect?" It is a call from Allah the Mighty and Majestic to His servants to reflect upon the signs. If you do not reflect upon the signs, know that you are deprived. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus 101].

Therefore, if you do not take heed from the signs, know that you are deprived and that your faith is deficient: ﴿But signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus 101]. So you, my brother, must reflect upon the signs of Allah: the cosmic signs of Allah and what is in this great universe of signs that point to His greatness, His dominion, His mercy, and His wisdom; and likewise the legislative signs of Allah. Whoever Allah grants understanding in the legislative signs benefits from them more than from the cosmic signs. When he contemplates what Allah has told us about Himself, His names, attributes, acts, and rulings, his faith in Allah the Mighty and Majestic increases, and through this he comes to know wisdom and mercy. When he contemplates what Allah has told us about the Last Day, and what occurs in it of reward, punishment, recompense, and reckoning, his faith likewise increases in Allah. Whenever a person reflects upon the legislative signs of Allah, his faith increases. Some blessed people find that their increase in faith through the legislative signs is greater than their increase through the cosmic signs. As for the person whom Allah opens up in both of these, how excellent that is.

...the sky, in it is our provision. So what is this provision of ours? Many scholars held that the provision mentioned here is rain, because God Most High said: ﴿It is He who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the sky. And none remembers except one who turns back [to Him].﴾ [Ghafir 13].

He said: ﴿And in the sky is your provision﴾, meaning the rain. Rain is called provision because it is the cause of provision. When God sends down rain, the earth brings forth water and pasture, as a provision for us and for our livestock. This is provision. How many people have their provision from what falls as rain: from crops, grasses, water and other things? Indeed, God Most High said: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink? Did you bring it down from the cloud, or are We the One who brings it down?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 68, 69].

Can anyone bring water down from the clouds? No, it is impossible. Can anyone create water in the clouds? No, it is impossible. God, Mighty and Majestic, is the One who undertakes that. This is the basis of provision; were it not for water, we would perish. Reflect on His saying, Most High: ﴿Did you bring it down from the cloud, or are We the One who brings it down? If We willed, We could make it salty and bitter, so why do you not give thanks?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 69, 70].

He did not say, "If We willed, We would not send it down", even though if He willed He would not send it down. Rather He said: ﴿If We willed, We could make it salty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 70], meaning: if We willed We would send it down, but We could make it salty, unfit to drink. A person's regret over water before him that he cannot drink or find palatable is greater than his regret over water that is missing, because water that is present but which you cannot benefit from or drink is a greater cause of regret than water that is lacking. For this reason God reminded us of this situation. Consider now: if this sweet, pure, pleasant rain became salty and bitter, what would the situation be? Very difficult indeed. Therefore He said: ﴿If We willed, We could make it salty, so why do you not give thanks?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 70].

He says: ﴿And in the sky is your provision﴾. So provision is the rain, as in the noble verse: ﴿and He sends down for you provision from the sky﴾ [Ghafir 13].

It may also be said that the provision in the sky is more general than that. It may be said that in the sky is our provision of rain, and what God has decreed for us in the Preserved Tablet of benefits and bodily advantages, such as wealth, children and other things. Thus this view is more comprehensive and general.

Know that the one who derives proofs from the Qur'an and the Sunnah should observe a useful rule: when we interpret a Qur'anic or Prophetic text, if we interpret it with a narrower meaning and interpret it with a more general meaning, which do we adopt? We adopt the second, the more general, because the more general includes the more specific, and not vice versa. Unless evidence indicates that it is specific, in which case the evidence is followed. But when no evidence indicates that, take the more general, because the more general includes the more specific and not vice versa. So here, if we say that the provision meant is more general than rain, the statement is correct, and it includes rain and other things.

His saying: ﴿and what you are promised﴾ means: and in it is what you are promised. What are we promised? We are promised Paradise. Paradise is in the sky, not on the earth. For this reason God Most High said in the story of Adam: ﴿We said: Go down from it﴾ [al-Baqarah 38], and descent is from above to below. So Paradise is in the sky. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed us that Paradise has degrees, and that the highest of them is al-Firdaws (the highest part of Paradise), and that it is both its highest and its middle part, indicating that the gardens are like a dome, whose highest point is its middle. He said: "From it gush forth the rivers of Paradise, and above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2530) and Ibn Majah (4331) from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal.]] So it is the highest thing. We ask God to make us and you among its dwellers, indeed He is over all things capable.

So what we are promised is Paradise. The provision is in the sky, and the Paradise that we are promised in the Hereafter is in the sky.

Thus we, the people of the earth, are in need of the sky in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. In the sky is our provision in this world, and in it is what we are promised in the Hereafter, which is Paradise. We ask God to make us and you among its people.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth, just as it is that you speak.﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 23]

The (fa') here is conjunctive (ʿātifah), the (waw) is for oath (lil-qasam), and ﴿Lord of the heaven and the earth﴾ is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He swore by Himself, Blessed and Exalted, on the basis of the requirement of His lordship over the heaven and the earth, that what they are promised is true. This is because He said: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision and what you are promised (22). So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is﴾, meaning: what you are promised. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, meaning: ﴿indeed it﴾, i.e., the Qur'an. It is also possible that it refers to the Prophet ﷺ. All three meanings are interrelated. His saying ﴿indeed it is the truth﴾ means: established and firm, because truth (al-haqq) and falsehood (al-batil) are opposites: falsehood is that which is vanished, lost, and aimless (sudan), while truth is that which is firm, which has benefit, and in which there is good and righteousness.

As for His saying ﴿just as it is that you speak﴾, it means: just as a person is certain of his speech, so this Qur'an is true. It is well known that none of us denies his own speech; when he speaks, he is certain that he spoke. So this Qur'an, the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is true, just as our speech is true.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Has there reached you the story of the honored guests of Abraham?﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 24]. ﴿Has there reached you﴾: is the address (al-khitab) only to the Prophet ﷺ? No, it is to him and to everyone to whom address can be directed and to whom it is valid to direct the address. It is as if He said: ﴿Has there reached you﴾, O listener, ﴿the story of the honored guests of Abraham﴾? The interrogative here is for arousing eagerness (tashwiq), just as it sometimes serves to instill fear (takhwif). Here, then, it is for arousing eagerness: it is as if He is making you eager to hear this story. Its counterpart in arousing eagerness is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ [as-Saff 10]. The intent of this interrogative is not that He is asking whether He will guide us, since one does not ask about his own act; rather, He wants to arouse the addressees' eagerness for that.

The interrogative may also be for threat, warning and intimidation, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Has there reached you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 1], then He said: ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled, labouring and exhausted﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 2, 3].

If someone says: What indicates to us that the interrogative is for arousing eagerness, or for threat, or for informing, or something similar? We say: what indicates this is the context (siyaq) and the circumstantial indicators (qara'in al-ahwal), and the intelligent person understands this and that.

﴿Has there reached you the story (hadith)﴾, that is, the news (khabar) of ﴿the guests of Abraham﴾. Here ﴿guests (dayf)﴾ is singular in form, but it applies to both the singular and the plural; they were a group of noble angels, peace be upon them. ﴿The guests of Abraham﴾ means those who descended as guests upon him. Abraham is the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, and he is the father of the Arabs and the father of the Children of Israel, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The religion of your father Abraham. He named you "the Muslims" before, and in this [Revelation]﴾ [al-Hajj 78]. He is the one whose religion Allah the Exalted commanded us to follow. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif, and he was not of those who associate others with Allah﴾ [an-Nahl 123].

For this reason the Jews claimed that Abraham was a Jew, and the Christians claimed that he was a Christian, but Allah the Exalted refuted them in that, saying: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a hanif, a Muslim, and he was not of those who associate others with Allah﴾ [Ali 'Imran 67].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 51, verse 25–30 (part 1 of 2):

The Exalted says: ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace!"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 25]. It is possible that ﴿when they entered﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿the honoured ones﴾, meaning: those whom he honoured when they entered upon him. It is also possible that it is the object of a verb that has been omitted, the implied meaning being: "Remember when they entered upon him." They entered upon Ibrahim, ﴿and said, "Peace!" He said, "Peace, a people unknown.﴾" ﴿They said, "Peace!"﴾ means: we greet you with peace. On this reading, ﴿Peace!﴾ (salaman) is a verbal noun whose governing verb is omitted, the implied meaning being "we say."

﴿He said, "Peace"﴾: ﴿Peace﴾ (salam) is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, the implied meaning being: "Peace be upon you." On this reading, the greeting here begins with a verbal sentence, while its reply is a nominal sentence, and the nominal sentence conveys permanence and continuity. For this reason the scholars, may God have mercy on them, said: Ibrahim's reply is more complete than the greeting of the angels, because the angels' greeting came in the verbal form, whereas Ibrahim's reply came in the nominal form.

﴿A people unknown﴾: ﴿a people﴾ (qawm) is the predicate of an omitted subject, the implied meaning being: "You are a people." He said they were a people because they appeared in human form. His saying ﴿unknown﴾ means: not recognised, as the Exalted says: ﴿But when he saw their hands not reaching towards it, he regarded them with suspicion and felt a fear of them﴾ [Hud 70].

In this verse there is evidence for the omission of the subject and the omission of the predicate. Where is the evidence for the omission of the predicate? ﴿Peace﴾, since we said the implied meaning is "Peace be upon you." The evidence for the omission of the subject is ﴿a people﴾, since the implied meaning is: "You are a people" (...).

﴿A people unknown (25). Then he turned quickly to his household﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 25, 26]. ﴿Turned quickly (fa-raagha)﴾ means slipped away secretly and swiftly. This was because of the goodness of his hospitality: he did not say, "Wait, I will bring you food," nor did he rise slowly as if being pushed; rather, he rose quickly and slipped away, lest they stand up when they saw him go to his family. It was as if he concealed the matter from them. ﴿He turned quickly to his household﴾ means: the people of his house. ﴿And brought a fattened calf﴾. In another verse: ﴿a roasted calf﴾ [Hud 69], meaning: grilled.

Meat, when it is roasted, is more savoury and tastier, because its flavour remains in it and does not mix with water. This is unlike when it is boiled: when it is boiled, its flavour mixes with the water and its pleasantness diminishes. But when it is roasted it becomes more delicious and better. ﴿A fattened calf﴾ means: he, peace be upon him, did not choose for his guests lean, emaciated beasts; rather, he chose for them fat beasts, since these are tastier, more tender and more nourishing. As for choosing a calf: either it was his peace be upon him custom to honour people in this way, or he honoured guests according to what the situation required. If they were many, he brought a calf; if they were fewer, he brought a sheep, and the like, according to the custom of generous people.

﴿Then he brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 27]. ﴿He brought it to them﴾ means: he did not place it far away, nor say, "Get up to your food"; rather he served them until he placed it before them. ﴿He brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ He did not say, "Eat!" Instead he presented it to them as an offer, because this is more emphatic in honour. Pay attention to this: an offer is gentler and kinder than a command, for if he had said, "Eat!" it could have been understood that he wished to assert superiority over them and direct a command at them. But he said, ﴿Will you not eat?﴾ You know the difference between the two expressions in gentleness: which is more delicate and more gracious?

﴿Will you not eat?﴾ Now, as you have seen, the food was brought near them. Do we say that the sunnah and the better course is that when a person invites guests, or guests come to him, he should bring the food to them in the sitting place? Or do we say that this varies according to circumstances? The second is more apparent, because the general statement of the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honour his guest" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6018) and Muslim (47/75) from Abu Hurayrah], indicates that you honour them with what custom has established as honouring. In our present custom, if you invite your companions and friends, and they are few, they do not consider serving food in their place of sitting to be an insult, because they are your brothers and friends, and the etiquette between you is lenient. But if a guest comes to you, or you invite a guest with whom you have no connection that removes, as they say, the formality of etiquette, then in our custom today it is not honouring him to serve food in the place of sitting, except out of necessity when you have no other place. Today honour consists in placing the food in a location, and then when you want them to eat it you say, "Please help yourselves, will you not help yourselves?" Or we change the setting, or the like of such common expressions.

The point, then, is that His saying, blessed and exalted, about Ibrahim: ﴿He brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ should be understood according to the custom of the people. If it is honouring to bring the food to the place where they sit, then bring it; if it is honouring to place it in another location, then do so. The evidence for this is His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honour his guest."

﴿Then he brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?" (27). Then he felt a fear of them﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 27, 28]. That is, he sensed within himself a fear of them. The cause of this fear was that when he, peace be upon him, set the food before them, they did not eat of it. ﴿He felt a fear of them﴾, because it is the custom that a guest eats what the host offers him. But these angels did not eat. They did not eat because the angels are ṣumm, meaning they have no bodies with hollow interiors, as has been transmitted from the early generations (salaf). For this reason they have no need of eating or drinking. ﴿He felt a fear of them. They said, "Do not fear"﴾: they reassured him, saying, "Do not fear," when they saw on his face the sign of denial and fear. Every person knows the state of the heart of the one facing him: is he in joy? Is he in contentment? Is he afraid? Is he at peace? For this is a matter known by natural disposition, and it does not require great insight.

﴿And they gave him the good news of a learned boy﴾ (al-bushra) is the report of what delights, that is, they informed him of what would please him: a learned boy. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had reached great old age before he had a son, he and his wife. They gave him good news of this boy, and gave him good news that he would be learned, meaning he would be a man of knowledge, because God the Exalted made him one of the prophets, and the prophets are the most knowledgeable of creation about God, the Mighty and Majestic, His names, His attributes, His rulings and His acts. This learned boy is not the same as the forbearing boy, for the Qur'an states that Ibrahim was given good news of a learned boy in two verses of the Book of God, and of a forbearing boy in one verse. They are two boys: the forbearing boy is Isma'il, father of the Arabs, and the learned boy is Ishaq, father of the Children of Israel. This is why you find their stories differ.

Whoever claims that the forbearing boy is the learned boy has strayed far from the truth. Indeed, there is a clear text in Surat as-Saffat: when the Exalted related the story of the sacrificed son in Surat as-Saffat, He said after it: ﴿And We gave him good news of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [as-Saffat 112]. How, then, would He give good news of one who (...)? All of this shows that the saying that the forbearing boy is not the learned boy is correct.

﴿They gave him the good news of a learned boy﴾. This is good news, as you see, and it contained good news of two things, or if you wish, say three things:
Firstly: that a child would come to him who would reach the stage of being a boy.
Secondly: that this child would be a male, not a female, as indicated by His saying ﴿boy﴾.
Thirdly: that he would be ﴿learned﴾, that is, possessed of knowledge. Each of these good tidings is great; each one alone would suffice as good news.

The Exalted says: ﴿They gave him the good news of a learned boy (28). Then his wife came forward with an outcry﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 28, 29]. Who was this wife? She was Sarah, mother of Ishaq. ﴿Came forward﴾ when she heard the good news. ﴿With an outcry﴾: a cry or a shout. Was it out of joy, or regret and sorrow? The answer: she came ﴿with an outcry﴾ out of joy, because this good news came to her after old age had advanced upon her. She cried out, and it was as if she was saying, God knows best, "A boy! A boy!" That is, she struck her hand as one astonished, as people still do today when news reaches them... God is greatest, and she struck her face.

﴿She struck her face and said, "A barren old woman!"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 29]. ﴿An old woman﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, the implied meaning being: "I am a barren old woman." It was as though she was amazed that this good news of a learned boy should come to her after old age had advanced and she had become barren of children. But they explained to her the one sole cause by which this child would come into being, and said: ﴿Thus says your Lord﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 30], meaning: just as we have said and given you good news, so said God, the Mighty and Majestic.

Consider His saying ﴿your Lord﴾, where He attributed lordship here to this aged, barren, elderly woman, as a sign that this is from God's care for her, because attributing lordship to a particular person is a special lordship. Pay attention to the difference: general lordship belongs to everyone, for God is Lord of all things; special lordship belongs only to one who is particularly devoted to God. Let me recite to you this verse: ﴿They said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun"﴾ [al-A'raf 121, 122].

General lordship is ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾; special lordship is ﴿Lord of Musa and Harun﴾. Here they said to her, ﴿Your Lord says﴾, by way of special lordship which entails special care. ﴿They said, "Thus says your Lord. Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 30], the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise﴾: you may take ﴿He﴾ here as a subject (mubtada'), with ﴿the All-Wise﴾ as its predicate. Or you may take ﴿He﴾ as a pronoun of separation (damir fasl), with ﴿the All-Wise﴾ as the predicate. The choice is yours. That is, if you wish, say: ﴿the All-Wise﴾ is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾, and ﴿He﴾ is a pronoun of separation that has no grammatical position (la mahalla lahu min al-i'rab). Or if you wish, say: ﴿He﴾ is a subject, and ﴿the All-Wise﴾ is the predicate of ﴿He﴾, and the whole clause is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. Here ﴿the All-Wise﴾ is placed before ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, because the context here calls for placing wisdom before knowledge.

The wisdom here lies in two things, brothers. Firstly: the delay of the birth in relation to this woman. God did not delay her giving birth until she reached old age except for a wisdom. Another wisdom lies in her giving birth after she had despaired and believed herself barren. So there are two wisdoms here: a prior wisdom and a subsequent wisdom. Therefore the name ﴿the All-Wise﴾ is placed before the name ﴿the All-Knowing﴾. You observe that when God combines these two noble names, "the All-Knowing" and "the All-Wise," the Qur'an generally puts "the All-Knowing" first, but here it puts ﴿the All-Wise﴾ first, because the context requires it: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾.

Here I ask: what is the meaning of ﴿the All-Wise﴾? Most people think that the meaning of "al-Hakim" is one who possesses wisdom, and wisdom is placing a thing in its proper place. But in fact ﴿al-Hakim﴾ has two meanings: "wise" from wisdom (hikmah), and "judging" from judgement (hukm). God the Mighty and Majestic is "wise" in the sense of wisdom, and He is also the Judge (al-Hakam) among His servants, the one who rules over them and judges between them. God the Exalted has said in the noble Qur'an: ﴿And who is better in judgement than God, for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50]. ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾ [at-Tin 8], and this interrogation is for affirmation, meaning that God is the most judicious of judges. In Surat al-Ma'idah He said: ﴿And who is better in judgement than God?﴾, while in Surat at-Tin: ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾

Both are in their proper place. In Surat al-Ma'idah God mentioned: ﴿Whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, they are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44], ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45], ﴿the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah 47], and the verses continue until He said: ﴿Do they seek the judgement of the age of ignorance? And who is better in judgement than God for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50]. So the context there is a comparison between rulings, and He makes clear that God's judgement is the best of judgements. But in Surat at-Tin the context is one of authority and power, and God is the most judicious of judges, meaning that His judgement is binding and His authority complete, and no one can oppose His judgement, however mighty his strength.

Consider the Exalted's saying about 'Ad: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the land without right and said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾ [Fussilat 15], meaning: none is mightier than us in strength. God said: ﴿Did they not see that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15], and He punished them with the most subtle of things. With what did He punish them? With the wind, the subtle air that you do not feel as touch, though when it is strong, air pushes everything away, and it is stronger than water, as is well known. With this subtle air He destroyed those people who said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?" [Fussilat 15]; He destroyed them with it.

The sum of it is that God is the most judicious of judges: His judgement is binding, proceeding from power and authority. Furthermore, "the most judicious of judges" also includes excellence of judgement.

So ﴿al-Hakim﴾ in His saying ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾ includes two meanings: a meaning from judgement (hukm) and a meaning from wisdom (hikmah). Having finished with judgement: the judgement of God the Mighty and Majestic includes that He is the Judge over His servants, that He is the one who judges between His servants, and that His judgement is the best of judgements, and that He, the Exalted, is the most judicious of judges.

As for wisdom: to God belongs perfect wisdom, and none of the acts existing in the universe is more judicious than God's wisdom. If you believe this, O believer, then many matters that trouble many people become easy for you, including some of the legal rulings whose wisdom most people, or some of them, do not grasp. Do we say, when we do not grasp the wisdom, that there is no wisdom in it, or do we say that it has a wisdom, but our intellects are limited? The second. When we believe in this way, we become content with many legal matters whose wisdom is hidden from us. Do we grasp the wisdom in the prayers being five? No. Or that they are seventeen rak'ahs? No.

Many legal matters have wisdoms that a person does not grasp. But when you believe that God is All-Wise, you believe that this matter must have a wisdom that requires it.

Likewise in matters of predestination: God may send a punishment that encompasses the righteous and the wicked, and He may send punishment upon a people from whom you would never expect punishment to come. Do you say, "What is the wisdom?" Or do you say that God the Mighty and Majestic's decree in this must proceed from wisdom? Therefore I tell you: our duty, regarding what God has commanded in the laws and what He has decreed in destinies, is to submit with complete submission, and not to object to it with our intellects.

Listen to the Exalted's saying: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves; then they find in themselves no discomfort from what you have judged and submit in full acceptance﴾ [an-Nisa' 65]. This is the first condition; ﴿then they find in themselves no discomfort from what you have judged﴾ is the second; the third is ﴿and submit in full acceptance﴾.

God the Mighty and Majestic swore that no one can believe unless he meets these three conditions: that they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves.

The second: that they find no discomfort in their hearts, meaning: their hearts are not constricted by God's judgement.

Third: that they submit with full submission. He emphasized this with the verbal noun ﴿تَسْلِيمًا﴾, meaning complete submission, without a person being lax or slow in carrying out God's ruling. If you find in yourself a defect related to these three matters, then correct your faith. If you find that you would like judgment to be sought from other than Allah and His Messenger, correct your faith. If you find in your heart that you want nothing but the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, yet your chest is constricted by the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, while you tell yourself that you could never seek judgment from other than Allah and His Messenger, but your chest is constricted, then correct your faith. If your chest is not constricted, you do not desire judgment from other than Allah and His Messenger, and your heart is open to the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, but you are slow and lax, then your faith is deficient. Read the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight away, as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ [al-An'am 110].

Because they did not believe in it the first time and did not accept it from the first time, their hearts became fluctuating (may Allah protect us), and Allah left them in their transgression, wandering blindly. Therefore, O believer, you must hasten with complete submission to the divine decree of Allah the Exalted (...).

* * *

...And may Allah's peace and blessings be upon our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and upon his family and companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

We had reached the words of Allah, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 31].

However, I decided to speak about the etiquettes of greeting, since the angels said: ﴿Peace﴾, and Abraham said: ﴿Peace﴾. We mentioned earlier that Abraham's response was better than the angels' greeting, because Abraham's response was a nominal sentence, which indicates permanence and continuity, unlike the angels' greeting. Know that returning a greeting is obligatory, based on the words of Allah, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it or return it.﴾ [an-Nisa' 86]. He said ﴿when you are greeted﴾ and did not mention who greets us, so it includes any person who greets us. We greet them back, responding with something better than their greeting or its equal, as He said: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it or return it.﴾ [an-Nisa' 86]. He began with "better," because it is the more excellent, then ﴿or return it﴾, meaning return its equivalent. This includes the case where a Jew, a Christian, a Buddhist, or others greet us; we return the greeting. However, we do not initiate greeting with Jews and Christians, because the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade that.[[Narrated by Muslim (2167/13) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

Furthermore, the greeting is said this way: "As-salamu 'alaykum" (Peace be upon you). This is what is prescribed. As for "Ahlan wa sahlan," "Marhaban," "How are you?" and the like, these are not prescribed. What is prescribed is that you begin with the greeting first. Therefore, in the hadith of the Mi'raj (the Night Ascension), when the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by the prophets and greeted them, he said: "He returned the greeting and said: 'Welcome, righteous Prophet.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (349) and Muslim (163/263) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]] So begin first by saying: "As-salamu 'alaykum." The reply should be like it or better: "Wa 'alaykumu as-salam," or "'Alaykum as-salam," or "'Alaykum as-salam wa rahmatullah," or "'Alaykum as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." All of this is prescribed. We see many people, when greeted, say: "Ahlan wa sahlan," or say "Marhaban, Abu so-and-so." This does not suffice. Even if he said, "Ahlan wa sahlan" for the rest of his life, it would not suffice, because Allah says: ﴿Greet with better than it or return it.﴾ [an-Nisa' 86]. It is well known that the one who says "as-salamu 'alayka" is invoking peace upon you from every deficiency, every affliction, and every sickness of the heart or body. It is not enough to say "Marhaban" and "Ahlan"; you must say "'Alayka as-salam" or "Wa 'alaykumu as-salam." If you add "wa rahmatullah wa barakatuh," it is better.

Second: who is required to greet first? The Sunnah (the recommended practice of the Prophet (ﷺ)) has explained this: "The young should greet the elderly,"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6231) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] because the elderly person's right is greater than the young person's right over the elderly. So the young person begins the greeting to the elderly. But if it is assumed that he does not greet, should the elderly person forgo the greeting because the right is his, or greet so that the Sunnah is not lost? The answer: he should greet, so that the Sunnah is not lost. For a person to say, "I am the one with the right; why did he not greet me?" is a mistake. It is true that you have the right, and that it is prescribed for him to greet you, but if he does not do so, then you greet. Likewise, "the one walking greets the one sitting," even if the sitting one is younger. If a person passes by someone seated, he should greet him, even if he is younger in age or status. It was part of the guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he would greet children when he passed by them.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6247) and Muslim (2168/14) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] In this there is great benefit:

Among them: humility, for a person lowers himself when he greets one who is beneath him.

Among them: mercy, for your greeting of the young is a form of mercy, and the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that the merciful are shown mercy by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4941) and al-Tirmidhi (1924) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As.]]

Among them: accustoming these children to greeting; that is, the child learns that the emblem of the Muslims is that they greet one another, and he takes from this a manner and character that benefits him in his youth and in his old age.

Third: the many greet the few, or the few greet the many: which of them has the greater right? The few, like the young with the elderly, greets the many. That is, when a group of five or six meet, who greets? The five greet the six, because the six have something more, and this extra has a right; the one who is more has a right. So the few greet the many. If they do not do so, then the many should greet the few, so that the Sunnah is not lost between them. Likewise, the rider and the walker: if two men meet, one walking and the other riding in his car or on his camel, who greets? The rider greets the walker, because the rider is higher, so he greets the walker, for the Sunnah came with this. Does the one ascending greet the one descending, or the one descending greet the one ascending? The one ascending greets the one descending. That is, if two people meet on a staircase, the one ascending is the one who greets the one descending. If the one who should initiate does not, then the second should initiate. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is not lawful for a Muslim to shun his brother for more than three days; when they meet, one turns away and the other turns away, and the better of them is the one who initiates the greeting."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6077) and Muslim (2560/25) from the hadith of Abu Ayyub.]] He said: "the better of them," which indicates that whoever initiates the greeting to another is better. This is so, because when you greet, you gain ten good deeds. Then, when your companion returns it, he gains ten good deeds. What is the cause that made him gain ten good deeds? The initiating cause. Had you not greeted, he would not have returned it. So you are the means for this one doing a righteous deed, and you have a share of its reward. For this reason the scholars said: initiating the greeting is a Sunnah, and returning it is obligatory. Then they raised a difficulty, saying: which is more excellent, initiating the greeting or returning it? Initiating the greeting is more excellent. Then they raised a difficulty, saying: how can the Sunnah be more excellent than the obligatory? The established legal principle is that the obligatory is more excellent, as Allah the Exalted said in the hadith qudsi (a hadith in which God speaks in the first person): "My servant draws near to Me with nothing more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6502) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

They answered this, saying: the answer to this difficulty is that this obligation was built upon the Sunnah. So the Sunnah upon which the obligation was built becomes, for the one who performs it, the reward of his specific act together with the reward of the obligatory reply.

Likewise, the greeting should be audible. Some people meet you and greet you, but you are unsure whether they greeted or not, because they did not raise their voice. This is an error. Raise your voice in a manner that shows you are pleased with this brother who met you, or whom you greeted, not with a jarring voice, nor with a voice so low that it cannot be heard. On the contrary, some people greet with a jarring voice, while the religion is a middle path between extremism and negligence. So we say: greet with a greeting that your brother can hear, and do so with courtesy and respect.

Among the etiquettes of greeting also: the one greeting should have a cheerful face and an open chest. It is well known that you should meet your brother with a radiant face.[[Narrated by Muslim (2626/144) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]] Radiance of face, openness of the chest, and a smile toward your brother are undoubtedly among the matters that are sought, because they bring joy to your brothers. Bringing joy to your brothers is among the recommended matters for which you are rewarded, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every act of kindness is charity."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6021) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah, and Muslim (1005/52) from the hadith of Huzayfah.]] Every act of kindness is charity.

If a greeting reaches you through a messenger, and the one who carries it is a person who says, "So-and-so sends you greetings," then say: "'Alayka wa 'alayhi as-salam" (Upon you and upon him be peace). If you wish, you may say: "'Alayhi as-salam," meaning upon the one who sent it.

As for a greeting conveyed in writing: that is, a person writes you a letter and says: "As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." If you want to reply by letter, respond to him in your reply. For example, a person wrote you a letter and said, "As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." When replying, you write: "J" (meaning "jawab," answer), "Wa 'alaykumu as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. I have read your letter and understood what is in it, and the answer is such and such." Most people now do not pay attention to this. You find them writing the reply and beginning with "As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah." This is good, but the one who greeted you wants a reply. Say: "J," meaning the answer: "Wa 'alaykumu as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Your letter reached me, or I read your letter and understood what is in it. This is the answer," and you answer what he asked. So when the greeting is written, its reply is in writing.

If it does not require a reply, such as when someone writes you a letter informing you of news that needs no answer, then when you read the letter, say: "'Alayka as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." I do not say it is obligatory, because your friend will not hear it, but it is a recommended act. If a man invokes blessings for you in your absence, then you invoke blessings for him in his absence.

Here the discussion of greeting ends.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 51, verse 25–30 (part 1 of 2):

The Exalted says: ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace!"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 25]. It is possible that ﴿when they entered﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿the honoured ones﴾, meaning: those whom he honoured when they entered upon him. It is also possible that it is the object of a verb that has been omitted, the implied meaning being: "Remember when they entered upon him." They entered upon Ibrahim, ﴿and said, "Peace!" He said, "Peace, a people unknown.﴾" ﴿They said, "Peace!"﴾ means: we greet you with peace. On this reading, ﴿Peace!﴾ (salaman) is a verbal noun whose governing verb is omitted, the implied meaning being "we say."

﴿He said, "Peace"﴾: ﴿Peace﴾ (salam) is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, the implied meaning being: "Peace be upon you." On this reading, the greeting here begins with a verbal sentence, while its reply is a nominal sentence, and the nominal sentence conveys permanence and continuity. For this reason the scholars, may God have mercy on them, said: Ibrahim's reply is more complete than the greeting of the angels, because the angels' greeting came in the verbal form, whereas Ibrahim's reply came in the nominal form.

﴿A people unknown﴾: ﴿a people﴾ (qawm) is the predicate of an omitted subject, the implied meaning being: "You are a people." He said they were a people because they appeared in human form. His saying ﴿unknown﴾ means: not recognised, as the Exalted says: ﴿But when he saw their hands not reaching towards it, he regarded them with suspicion and felt a fear of them﴾ [Hud 70].

In this verse there is evidence for the omission of the subject and the omission of the predicate. Where is the evidence for the omission of the predicate? ﴿Peace﴾, since we said the implied meaning is "Peace be upon you." The evidence for the omission of the subject is ﴿a people﴾, since the implied meaning is: "You are a people" (...).

﴿A people unknown (25). Then he turned quickly to his household﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 25, 26]. ﴿Turned quickly (fa-raagha)﴾ means slipped away secretly and swiftly. This was because of the goodness of his hospitality: he did not say, "Wait, I will bring you food," nor did he rise slowly as if being pushed; rather, he rose quickly and slipped away, lest they stand up when they saw him go to his family. It was as if he concealed the matter from them. ﴿He turned quickly to his household﴾ means: the people of his house. ﴿And brought a fattened calf﴾. In another verse: ﴿a roasted calf﴾ [Hud 69], meaning: grilled.

Meat, when it is roasted, is more savoury and tastier, because its flavour remains in it and does not mix with water. This is unlike when it is boiled: when it is boiled, its flavour mixes with the water and its pleasantness diminishes. But when it is roasted it becomes more delicious and better. ﴿A fattened calf﴾ means: he, peace be upon him, did not choose for his guests lean, emaciated beasts; rather, he chose for them fat beasts, since these are tastier, more tender and more nourishing. As for choosing a calf: either it was his peace be upon him custom to honour people in this way, or he honoured guests according to what the situation required. If they were many, he brought a calf; if they were fewer, he brought a sheep, and the like, according to the custom of generous people.

﴿Then he brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 27]. ﴿He brought it to them﴾ means: he did not place it far away, nor say, "Get up to your food"; rather he served them until he placed it before them. ﴿He brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ He did not say, "Eat!" Instead he presented it to them as an offer, because this is more emphatic in honour. Pay attention to this: an offer is gentler and kinder than a command, for if he had said, "Eat!" it could have been understood that he wished to assert superiority over them and direct a command at them. But he said, ﴿Will you not eat?﴾ You know the difference between the two expressions in gentleness: which is more delicate and more gracious?

﴿Will you not eat?﴾ Now, as you have seen, the food was brought near them. Do we say that the sunnah and the better course is that when a person invites guests, or guests come to him, he should bring the food to them in the sitting place? Or do we say that this varies according to circumstances? The second is more apparent, because the general statement of the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honour his guest" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6018) and Muslim (47/75) from Abu Hurayrah], indicates that you honour them with what custom has established as honouring. In our present custom, if you invite your companions and friends, and they are few, they do not consider serving food in their place of sitting to be an insult, because they are your brothers and friends, and the etiquette between you is lenient. But if a guest comes to you, or you invite a guest with whom you have no connection that removes, as they say, the formality of etiquette, then in our custom today it is not honouring him to serve food in the place of sitting, except out of necessity when you have no other place. Today honour consists in placing the food in a location, and then when you want them to eat it you say, "Please help yourselves, will you not help yourselves?" Or we change the setting, or the like of such common expressions.

The point, then, is that His saying, blessed and exalted, about Ibrahim: ﴿He brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ should be understood according to the custom of the people. If it is honouring to bring the food to the place where they sit, then bring it; if it is honouring to place it in another location, then do so. The evidence for this is His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honour his guest."

﴿Then he brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?" (27). Then he felt a fear of them﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 27, 28]. That is, he sensed within himself a fear of them. The cause of this fear was that when he, peace be upon him, set the food before them, they did not eat of it. ﴿He felt a fear of them﴾, because it is the custom that a guest eats what the host offers him. But these angels did not eat. They did not eat because the angels are ṣumm, meaning they have no bodies with hollow interiors, as has been transmitted from the early generations (salaf). For this reason they have no need of eating or drinking. ﴿He felt a fear of them. They said, "Do not fear"﴾: they reassured him, saying, "Do not fear," when they saw on his face the sign of denial and fear. Every person knows the state of the heart of the one facing him: is he in joy? Is he in contentment? Is he afraid? Is he at peace? For this is a matter known by natural disposition, and it does not require great insight.

﴿And they gave him the good news of a learned boy﴾ (al-bushra) is the report of what delights, that is, they informed him of what would please him: a learned boy. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had reached great old age before he had a son, he and his wife. They gave him good news of this boy, and gave him good news that he would be learned, meaning he would be a man of knowledge, because God the Exalted made him one of the prophets, and the prophets are the most knowledgeable of creation about God, the Mighty and Majestic, His names, His attributes, His rulings and His acts. This learned boy is not the same as the forbearing boy, for the Qur'an states that Ibrahim was given good news of a learned boy in two verses of the Book of God, and of a forbearing boy in one verse. They are two boys: the forbearing boy is Isma'il, father of the Arabs, and the learned boy is Ishaq, father of the Children of Israel. This is why you find their stories differ.

Whoever claims that the forbearing boy is the learned boy has strayed far from the truth. Indeed, there is a clear text in Surat as-Saffat: when the Exalted related the story of the sacrificed son in Surat as-Saffat, He said after it: ﴿And We gave him good news of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [as-Saffat 112]. How, then, would He give good news of one who (...)? All of this shows that the saying that the forbearing boy is not the learned boy is correct.

﴿They gave him the good news of a learned boy﴾. This is good news, as you see, and it contained good news of two things, or if you wish, say three things:
Firstly: that a child would come to him who would reach the stage of being a boy.
Secondly: that this child would be a male, not a female, as indicated by His saying ﴿boy﴾.
Thirdly: that he would be ﴿learned﴾, that is, possessed of knowledge. Each of these good tidings is great; each one alone would suffice as good news.

The Exalted says: ﴿They gave him the good news of a learned boy (28). Then his wife came forward with an outcry﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 28, 29]. Who was this wife? She was Sarah, mother of Ishaq. ﴿Came forward﴾ when she heard the good news. ﴿With an outcry﴾: a cry or a shout. Was it out of joy, or regret and sorrow?
