On this reading, the greeting here begins with a verbal sentence, while its reply is a nominal sentence, and the nominal sentence conveys permanence and continuity. For this reason the scholars, may God have mercy on them, said: Ibrahim's reply is more complete than the greeting of the angels, because the angels' greeting came in the verbal form, whereas Ibrahim's reply came in the nominal form.

﴿A people unknown﴾: ﴿a people﴾ (qawm) is the predicate of an omitted subject, the implied meaning being: "You are a people." He said they were a people because they appeared in human form. His saying ﴿unknown﴾ means: not recognised, as the Exalted says: ﴿But when he saw their hands not reaching towards it, he regarded them with suspicion and felt a fear of them﴾ [Hud 70].

In this verse there is evidence for the omission of the subject and the omission of the predicate. Where is the evidence for the omission of the predicate? ﴿Peace﴾, since we said the implied meaning is "Peace be upon you." The evidence for the omission of the subject is ﴿a people﴾, since the implied meaning is: "You are a people" (...).

﴿A people unknown (25). Then he turned quickly to his household﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 25, 26]. ﴿Turned quickly (fa-raagha)﴾ means slipped away secretly and swiftly. This was because of the goodness of his hospitality: he did not say, "Wait, I will bring you food," nor did he rise slowly as if being pushed; rather, he rose quickly and slipped away, lest they stand up when they saw him go to his family. It was as if he concealed the matter from them. ﴿He turned quickly to his household﴾ means: the people of his house. ﴿And brought a fattened calf﴾. In another verse: ﴿a roasted calf﴾ [Hud 69], meaning: grilled.

Meat, when it is roasted, is more savoury and tastier, because its flavour remains in it and does not mix with water. This is unlike when it is boiled: when it is boiled, its flavour mixes with the water and its pleasantness diminishes. But when it is roasted it becomes more delicious and better. ﴿A fattened calf﴾ means: he, peace be upon him, did not choose for his guests lean, emaciated beasts; rather, he chose for them fat beasts, since these are tastier, more tender and more nourishing. As for choosing a calf: either it was his peace be upon him custom to honour people in this way, or he honoured guests according to what the situation required. If they were many, he brought a calf; if they were fewer, he brought a sheep, and the like, according to the custom of generous people.

﴿Then he brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 27]. ﴿He brought it to them﴾ means: he did not place it far away, nor say, "Get up to your food"; rather he served them until he placed it before them. ﴿He brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ He did not say, "Eat!" Instead he presented it to them as an offer, because this is more emphatic in honour. Pay attention to this: an offer is gentler and kinder than a command, for if he had said, "Eat!" it could have been understood that he wished to assert superiority over them and direct a command at them. But he said, ﴿Will you not eat?﴾ You know the difference between the two expressions in gentleness: which is more delicate and more gracious?

﴿Will you not eat?﴾ Now, as you have seen, the food was brought near them. Do we say that the sunnah and the better course is that when a person invites guests, or guests come to him, he should bring the food to them in the sitting place? Or do we say that this varies according to circumstances? The second is more apparent, because the general statement of the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honour his guest" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6018) and Muslim (47/75) from Abu Hurayrah], indicates that you honour them with what custom has established as honouring. In our present custom, if you invite your companions and friends, and they are few, they do not consider serving food in their place of sitting to be an insult, because they are your brothers and friends, and the etiquette between you is lenient. But if a guest comes to you, or you invite a guest with whom you have no connection that removes, as they say, the formality of etiquette, then in our custom today it is not honouring him to serve food in the place of sitting, except out of necessity when you have no other place. Today honour consists in placing the food in a location, and then when you want them to eat it you say, "Please help yourselves, will you not help yourselves?" Or we change the setting, or the like of such common expressions.

The point, then, is that His saying, blessed and exalted, about Ibrahim: ﴿He brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ should be understood according to the custom of the people. If it is honouring to bring the food to the place where they sit, then bring it; if it is honouring to place it in another location, then do so. The evidence for this is His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honour his guest."

﴿Then he brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?" (27). Then he felt a fear of them﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 27, 28]. That is, he sensed within himself a fear of them. The cause of this fear was that when he, peace be upon him, set the food before them, they did not eat of it. ﴿He felt a fear of them﴾, because it is the custom that a guest eats what the host offers him. But these angels did not eat. They did not eat because the angels are ṣumm, meaning they have no bodies with hollow interiors, as has been transmitted from the early generations (salaf). For this reason they have no need of eating or drinking. ﴿He felt a fear of them. They said, "Do not fear"﴾: they reassured him, saying, "Do not fear," when they saw on his face the sign of denial and fear. Every person knows the state of the heart of the one facing him: is he in joy? Is he in contentment? Is he afraid? Is he at peace? For this is a matter known by natural disposition, and it does not require great insight.

﴿And they gave him the good news of a learned boy﴾ (al-bushra) is the report of what delights, that is, they informed him of what would please him: a learned boy. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had reached great old age before he had a son, he and his wife. They gave him good news of this boy, and gave him good news that he would be learned, meaning he would be a man of knowledge, because God the Exalted made him one of the prophets, and the prophets are the most knowledgeable of creation about God, the Mighty and Majestic, His names, His attributes, His rulings and His acts. This learned boy is not the same as the forbearing boy, for the Qur'an states that Ibrahim was given good news of a learned boy in two verses of the Book of God, and of a forbearing boy in one verse. They are two boys: the forbearing boy is Isma'il, father of the Arabs, and the learned boy is Ishaq, father of the Children of Israel. This is why you find their stories differ.

Whoever claims that the forbearing boy is the learned boy has strayed far from the truth. Indeed, there is a clear text in Surat as-Saffat: when the Exalted related the story of the sacrificed son in Surat as-Saffat, He said after it: ﴿And We gave him good news of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [as-Saffat 112]. How, then, would He give good news of one who (...)? All of this shows that the saying that the forbearing boy is not the learned boy is correct.

﴿They gave him the good news of a learned boy﴾. This is good news, as you see, and it contained good news of two things, or if you wish, say three things:
Firstly: that a child would come to him who would reach the stage of being a boy.
Secondly: that this child would be a male, not a female, as indicated by His saying ﴿boy﴾.
Thirdly: that he would be ﴿learned﴾, that is, possessed of knowledge. Each of these good tidings is great; each one alone would suffice as good news.

The Exalted says: ﴿They gave him the good news of a learned boy (28). Then his wife came forward with an outcry﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 28, 29]. Who was this wife? She was Sarah, mother of Ishaq. ﴿Came forward﴾ when she heard the good news. ﴿With an outcry﴾: a cry or a shout. Was it out of joy, or regret and sorrow? The answer: she came ﴿with an outcry﴾ out of joy, because this good news came to her after old age had advanced upon her. She cried out, and it was as if she was saying, God knows best, "A boy! A boy!" That is, she struck her hand as one astonished, as people still do today when news reaches them... God is greatest, and she struck her face.

﴿She struck her face and said, "A barren old woman!"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 29]. ﴿An old woman﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, the implied meaning being: "I am a barren old woman." It was as though she was amazed that this good news of a learned boy should come to her after old age had advanced and she had become barren of children. But they explained to her the one sole cause by which this child would come into being, and said: ﴿Thus says your Lord﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 30], meaning: just as we have said and given you good news, so said God, the Mighty and Majestic.

Consider His saying ﴿your Lord﴾, where He attributed lordship here to this aged, barren, elderly woman, as a sign that this is from God's care for her, because attributing lordship to a particular person is a special lordship. Pay attention to the difference: general lordship belongs to everyone, for God is Lord of all things; special lordship belongs only to one who is particularly devoted to God. Let me recite to you this verse: ﴿They said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun"﴾ [al-A'raf 121, 122].

General lordship is ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾; special lordship is ﴿Lord of Musa and Harun﴾. Here they said to her, ﴿Your Lord says﴾, by way of special lordship which entails special care. ﴿They said, "Thus says your Lord. Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 30], the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise﴾: you may take ﴿He﴾ here as a subject (mubtada'), with ﴿the All-Wise﴾ as its predicate. Or you may take ﴿He﴾ as a pronoun of separation (damir fasl), with ﴿the All-Wise﴾ as the predicate. The choice is yours. That is, if you wish, say: ﴿the All-Wise﴾ is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾, and ﴿He﴾ is a pronoun of separation that has no grammatical position (la mahalla lahu min al-i'rab). Or if you wish, say: ﴿He﴾ is a subject, and ﴿the All-Wise﴾ is the predicate of ﴿He﴾, and the whole clause is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. Here ﴿the All-Wise﴾ is placed before ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, because the context here calls for placing wisdom before knowledge.

The wisdom here lies in two things, brothers. Firstly: the delay of the birth in relation to this woman. God did not delay her giving birth until she reached old age except for a wisdom. Another wisdom lies in her giving birth after she had despaired and believed herself barren. So there are two wisdoms here: a prior wisdom and a subsequent wisdom. Therefore the name ﴿the All-Wise﴾ is placed before the name ﴿the All-Knowing﴾. You observe that when God combines these two noble names, "the All-Knowing" and "the All-Wise," the Qur'an generally puts "the All-Knowing" first, but here it puts ﴿the All-Wise﴾ first, because the context requires it: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾.

Here I ask: what is the meaning of ﴿the All-Wise﴾? Most people think that the meaning of "al-Hakim" is one who possesses wisdom, and wisdom is placing a thing in its proper place. But in fact ﴿al-Hakim﴾ has two meanings: "wise" from wisdom (hikmah), and "judging" from judgement (hukm). God the Mighty and Majestic is "wise" in the sense of wisdom, and He is also the Judge (al-Hakam) among His servants, the one who rules over them and judges between them. God the Exalted has said in the noble Qur'an: ﴿And who is better in judgement than God, for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50]. ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾ [at-Tin 8], and this interrogation is for affirmation, meaning that God is the most judicious of judges. In Surat al-Ma'idah He said: ﴿And who is better in judgement than God?﴾, while in Surat at-Tin: ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾

Both are in their proper place. In Surat al-Ma'idah God mentioned: ﴿Whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, they are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44], ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45], ﴿the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah 47], and the verses continue until He said: ﴿Do they seek the judgement of the age of ignorance? And who is better in judgement than God for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50]. So the context there is a comparison between rulings, and He makes clear that God's judgement is the best of judgements. But in Surat at-Tin the context is one of authority and power, and God is the most judicious of judges, meaning that His judgement is binding and His authority complete, and no one can oppose His judgement, however mighty his strength.

Consider the Exalted's saying about 'Ad: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the land without right and said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾ [Fussilat 15], meaning: none is mightier than us in strength. God said: ﴿Did they not see that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15], and He punished them with the most subtle of things. With what did He punish them? With the wind, the subtle air that you do not feel as touch, though when it is strong, air pushes everything away, and it is stronger than water, as is well known. With this subtle air He destroyed those people who said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?" [Fussilat 15]; He destroyed them with it.

The sum of it is that God is the most judicious of judges: His judgement is binding, proceeding from power and authority. Furthermore, "the most judicious of judges" also includes excellence of judgement.

So ﴿al-Hakim﴾ in His saying ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾ includes two meanings: a meaning from judgement (hukm) and a meaning from wisdom (hikmah). Having finished with judgement: the judgement of God the Mighty and Majestic includes that He is the Judge over His servants, that He is the one who judges between His servants, and that His judgement is the best of judgements, and that He, the Exalted, is the most judicious of judges.

As for wisdom: to God belongs perfect wisdom, and none of the acts existing in the universe is more judicious than God's wisdom. If you believe this, O believer, then many matters that trouble many people become easy for you, including some of the legal rulings whose wisdom most people, or some of them, do not grasp. Do we say, when we do not grasp the wisdom, that there is no wisdom in it, or do we say that it has a wisdom, but our intellects are limited? The second. When we believe in this way, we become content with many legal matters whose wisdom is hidden from us. Do we grasp the wisdom in the prayers being five? No. Or that they are seventeen rak'ahs? No.

Many legal matters have wisdoms that a person does not grasp. But when you believe that God is All-Wise, you believe that this matter must have a wisdom that requires it.

Likewise in matters of predestination: God may send a punishment that encompasses the righteous and the wicked, and He may send punishment upon a people from whom you would never expect punishment to come. Do you say, "What is the wisdom?" Or do you say that God the Mighty and Majestic's decree in this must proceed from wisdom? Therefore I tell you: our duty, regarding what God has commanded in the laws and what He has decreed in destinies, is to submit with complete submission, and not to object to it with our intellects.

Listen to the Exalted's saying: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves; then they find in themselves no discomfort from what you have judged and submit in full acceptance﴾ [an-Nisa' 65]. This is the first condition; ﴿then they find in themselves no discomfort from what you have judged﴾ is the second; the third is ﴿and submit in full acceptance﴾.

God the Mighty and Majestic swore that no one can believe unless he meets these three conditions: that they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves.

The second: that they find no discomfort in their hearts, meaning: their hearts are not constricted by God's judgement.

Third: that they submit with full submission. He emphasized this with the verbal noun ﴿تَسْلِيمًا﴾, meaning complete submission, without a person being lax or slow in carrying out God's ruling. If you find in yourself a defect related to these three matters, then correct your faith. If you find that you would like judgment to be sought from other than Allah and His Messenger, correct your faith. If you find in your heart that you want nothing but the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, yet your chest is constricted by the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, while you tell yourself that you could never seek judgment from other than Allah and His Messenger, but your chest is constricted, then correct your faith. If your chest is not constricted, you do not desire judgment from other than Allah and His Messenger, and your heart is open to the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, but you are slow and lax, then your faith is deficient. Read the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight away, as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ [al-An'am 110].

Because they did not believe in it the first time and did not accept it from the first time, their hearts became fluctuating (may Allah protect us), and Allah left them in their transgression, wandering blindly. Therefore, O believer, you must hasten with complete submission to the divine decree of Allah the Exalted (...).

* * *

...And may Allah's peace and blessings be upon our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and upon his family and companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

We had reached the words of Allah, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 31].

However, I decided to speak about the etiquettes of greeting, since the angels said: ﴿Peace﴾, and Abraham said: ﴿Peace﴾. We mentioned earlier that Abraham's response was better than the angels' greeting, because Abraham's response was a nominal sentence, which indicates permanence and continuity, unlike the angels' greeting. Know that returning a greeting is obligatory, based on the words of Allah, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it or return it.﴾ [an-Nisa' 86]. He said ﴿when you are greeted﴾ and did not mention who greets us, so it includes any person who greets us. We greet them back, responding with something better than their greeting or its equal, as He said: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it or return it.﴾ [an-Nisa' 86]. He began with "better," because it is the more excellent, then ﴿or return it﴾, meaning return its equivalent. This includes the case where a Jew, a Christian, a Buddhist, or others greet us; we return the greeting. However, we do not initiate greeting with Jews and Christians, because the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade that.[[Narrated by Muslim (2167/13) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

Furthermore, the greeting is said this way: "As-salamu 'alaykum" (Peace be upon you). This is what is prescribed. As for "Ahlan wa sahlan," "Marhaban," "How are you?" and the like, these are not prescribed. What is prescribed is that you begin with the greeting first. Therefore, in the hadith of the Mi'raj (the Night Ascension), when the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by the prophets and greeted them, he said: "He returned the greeting and said: 'Welcome, righteous Prophet.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (349) and Muslim (163/263) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]] So begin first by saying: "As-salamu 'alaykum." The reply should be like it or better: "Wa 'alaykumu as-salam," or "'Alaykum as-salam," or "'Alaykum as-salam wa rahmatullah," or "'Alaykum as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." All of this is prescribed. We see many people, when greeted, say: "Ahlan wa sahlan," or say "Marhaban, Abu so-and-so." This does not suffice. Even if he said, "Ahlan wa sahlan" for the rest of his life, it would not suffice, because Allah says: ﴿Greet with better than it or return it.﴾ [an-Nisa' 86]. It is well known that the one who says "as-salamu 'alayka" is invoking peace upon you from every deficiency, every affliction, and every sickness of the heart or body. It is not enough to say "Marhaban" and "Ahlan"; you must say "'Alayka as-salam" or "Wa 'alaykumu as-salam." If you add "wa rahmatullah wa barakatuh," it is better.

Second: who is required to greet first? The Sunnah (the recommended practice of the Prophet (ﷺ)) has explained this: "The young should greet the elderly,"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6231) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] because the elderly person's right is greater than the young person's right over the elderly. So the young person begins the greeting to the elderly. But if it is assumed that he does not greet, should the elderly person forgo the greeting because the right is his, or greet so that the Sunnah is not lost? The answer: he should greet, so that the Sunnah is not lost. For a person to say, "I am the one with the right; why did he not greet me?" is a mistake. It is true that you have the right, and that it is prescribed for him to greet you, but if he does not do so, then you greet. Likewise, "the one walking greets the one sitting," even if the sitting one is younger. If a person passes by someone seated, he should greet him, even if he is younger in age or status. It was part of the guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he would greet children when he passed by them.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6247) and Muslim (2168/14) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] In this there is great benefit:

Among them: humility, for a person lowers himself when he greets one who is beneath him.

Among them: mercy, for your greeting of the young is a form of mercy, and the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that the merciful are shown mercy by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4941) and al-Tirmidhi (1924) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As.]]

Among them: accustoming these children to greeting; that is, the child learns that the emblem of the Muslims is that they greet one another, and he takes from this a manner and character that benefits him in his youth and in his old age.

Third: the many greet the few, or the few greet the many: which of them has the greater right? The few, like the young with the elderly, greets the many. That is, when a group of five or six meet, who greets? The five greet the six, because the six have something more, and this extra has a right; the one who is more has a right. So the few greet the many. If they do not do so, then the many should greet the few, so that the Sunnah is not lost between them. Likewise, the rider and the walker: if two men meet, one walking and the other riding in his car or on his camel, who greets? The rider greets the walker, because the rider is higher, so he greets the walker, for the Sunnah came with this. Does the one ascending greet the one descending, or the one descending greet the one ascending? The one ascending greets the one descending. That is, if two people meet on a staircase, the one ascending is the one who greets the one descending. If the one who should initiate does not, then the second should initiate. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is not lawful for a Muslim to shun his brother for more than three days; when they meet, one turns away and the other turns away, and the better of them is the one who initiates the greeting."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6077) and Muslim (2560/25) from the hadith of Abu Ayyub.]] He said: "the better of them," which indicates that whoever initiates the greeting to another is better. This is so, because when you greet, you gain ten good deeds. Then, when your companion returns it, he gains ten good deeds. What is the cause that made him gain ten good deeds? The initiating cause. Had you not greeted, he would not have returned it. So you are the means for this one doing a righteous deed, and you have a share of its reward. For this reason the scholars said: initiating the greeting is a Sunnah, and returning it is obligatory. Then they raised a difficulty, saying: which is more excellent, initiating the greeting or returning it? Initiating the greeting is more excellent. Then they raised a difficulty, saying: how can the Sunnah be more excellent than the obligatory? The established legal principle is that the obligatory is more excellent, as Allah the Exalted said in the hadith qudsi (a hadith in which God speaks in the first person): "My servant draws near to Me with nothing more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6502) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

They answered this, saying: the answer to this difficulty is that this obligation was built upon the Sunnah. So the Sunnah upon which the obligation was built becomes, for the one who performs it, the reward of his specific act together with the reward of the obligatory reply.

Likewise, the greeting should be audible. Some people meet you and greet you, but you are unsure whether they greeted or not, because they did not raise their voice. This is an error. Raise your voice in a manner that shows you are pleased with this brother who met you, or whom you greeted, not with a jarring voice, nor with a voice so low that it cannot be heard. On the contrary, some people greet with a jarring voice, while the religion is a middle path between extremism and negligence. So we say: greet with a greeting that your brother can hear, and do so with courtesy and respect.

Among the etiquettes of greeting also: the one greeting should have a cheerful face and an open chest. It is well known that you should meet your brother with a radiant face.[[Narrated by Muslim (2626/144) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]] Radiance of face, openness of the chest, and a smile toward your brother are undoubtedly among the matters that are sought, because they bring joy to your brothers. Bringing joy to your brothers is among the recommended matters for which you are rewarded, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every act of kindness is charity."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6021) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah, and Muslim (1005/52) from the hadith of Huzayfah.]] Every act of kindness is charity.

If a greeting reaches you through a messenger, and the one who carries it is a person who says, "So-and-so sends you greetings," then say: "'Alayka wa 'alayhi as-salam" (Upon you and upon him be peace). If you wish, you may say: "'Alayhi as-salam," meaning upon the one who sent it.

As for a greeting conveyed in writing: that is, a person writes you a letter and says: "As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." If you want to reply by letter, respond to him in your reply. For example, a person wrote you a letter and said, "As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." When replying, you write: "J" (meaning "jawab," answer), "Wa 'alaykumu as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. I have read your letter and understood what is in it, and the answer is such and such." Most people now do not pay attention to this. You find them writing the reply and beginning with "As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah." This is good, but the one who greeted you wants a reply. Say: "J," meaning the answer: "Wa 'alaykumu as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Your letter reached me, or I read your letter and understood what is in it. This is the answer," and you answer what he asked. So when the greeting is written, its reply is in writing.

If it does not require a reply, such as when someone writes you a letter informing you of news that needs no answer, then when you read the letter, say: "'Alayka as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." I do not say it is obligatory, because your friend will not hear it, but it is a recommended act. If a man invokes blessings for you in your absence, then you invoke blessings for him in his absence.

Here the discussion of greeting ends.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 51, verse 25–30 (part 1 of 2):

The Exalted says: ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace!"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 25]. It is possible that ﴿when they entered﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿the honoured ones﴾, meaning: those whom he honoured when they entered upon him. It is also possible that it is the object of a verb that has been omitted, the implied meaning being: "Remember when they entered upon him." They entered upon Ibrahim, ﴿and said, "Peace!" He said, "Peace, a people unknown.﴾" ﴿They said, "Peace!"﴾ means: we greet you with peace. On this reading, ﴿Peace!﴾ (salaman) is a verbal noun whose governing verb is omitted, the implied meaning being "we say."

﴿He said, "Peace"﴾: ﴿Peace﴾ (salam) is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, the implied meaning being: "Peace be upon you." On this reading, the greeting here begins with a verbal sentence, while its reply is a nominal sentence, and the nominal sentence conveys permanence and continuity. For this reason the scholars, may God have mercy on them, said: Ibrahim's reply is more complete than the greeting of the angels, because the angels' greeting came in the verbal form, whereas Ibrahim's reply came in the nominal form.

﴿A people unknown﴾: ﴿a people﴾ (qawm) is the predicate of an omitted subject, the implied meaning being: "You are a people." He said they were a people because they appeared in human form. His saying ﴿unknown﴾ means: not recognised, as the Exalted says: ﴿But when he saw their hands not reaching towards it, he regarded them with suspicion and felt a fear of them﴾ [Hud 70].

In this verse there is evidence for the omission of the subject and the omission of the predicate. Where is the evidence for the omission of the predicate? ﴿Peace﴾, since we said the implied meaning is "Peace be upon you." The evidence for the omission of the subject is ﴿a people﴾, since the implied meaning is: "You are a people" (...).

﴿A people unknown (25). Then he turned quickly to his household﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 25, 26]. ﴿Turned quickly (fa-raagha)﴾ means slipped away secretly and swiftly. This was because of the goodness of his hospitality: he did not say, "Wait, I will bring you food," nor did he rise slowly as if being pushed; rather, he rose quickly and slipped away, lest they stand up when they saw him go to his family. It was as if he concealed the matter from them. ﴿He turned quickly to his household﴾ means: the people of his house. ﴿And brought a fattened calf﴾. In another verse: ﴿a roasted calf﴾ [Hud 69], meaning: grilled.

Meat, when it is roasted, is more savoury and tastier, because its flavour remains in it and does not mix with water. This is unlike when it is boiled: when it is boiled, its flavour mixes with the water and its pleasantness diminishes. But when it is roasted it becomes more delicious and better. ﴿A fattened calf﴾ means: he, peace be upon him, did not choose for his guests lean, emaciated beasts; rather, he chose for them fat beasts, since these are tastier, more tender and more nourishing. As for choosing a calf: either it was his peace be upon him custom to honour people in this way, or he honoured guests according to what the situation required. If they were many, he brought a calf; if they were fewer, he brought a sheep, and the like, according to the custom of generous people.

﴿Then he brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 27]. ﴿He brought it to them﴾ means: he did not place it far away, nor say, "Get up to your food"; rather he served them until he placed it before them. ﴿He brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ He did not say, "Eat!" Instead he presented it to them as an offer, because this is more emphatic in honour. Pay attention to this: an offer is gentler and kinder than a command, for if he had said, "Eat!" it could have been understood that he wished to assert superiority over them and direct a command at them. But he said, ﴿Will you not eat?﴾ You know the difference between the two expressions in gentleness: which is more delicate and more gracious?

﴿Will you not eat?﴾ Now, as you have seen, the food was brought near them. Do we say that the sunnah and the better course is that when a person invites guests, or guests come to him, he should bring the food to them in the sitting place? Or do we say that this varies according to circumstances? The second is more apparent, because the general statement of the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honour his guest" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6018) and Muslim (47/75) from Abu Hurayrah], indicates that you honour them with what custom has established as honouring. In our present custom, if you invite your companions and friends, and they are few, they do not consider serving food in their place of sitting to be an insult, because they are your brothers and friends, and the etiquette between you is lenient. But if a guest comes to you, or you invite a guest with whom you have no connection that removes, as they say, the formality of etiquette, then in our custom today it is not honouring him to serve food in the place of sitting, except out of necessity when you have no other place. Today honour consists in placing the food in a location, and then when you want them to eat it you say, "Please help yourselves, will you not help yourselves?" Or we change the setting, or the like of such common expressions.

The point, then, is that His saying, blessed and exalted, about Ibrahim: ﴿He brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ should be understood according to the custom of the people. If it is honouring to bring the food to the place where they sit, then bring it; if it is honouring to place it in another location, then do so. The evidence for this is His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honour his guest."

﴿Then he brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?" (27). Then he felt a fear of them﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 27, 28]. That is, he sensed within himself a fear of them. The cause of this fear was that when he, peace be upon him, set the food before them, they did not eat of it. ﴿He felt a fear of them﴾, because it is the custom that a guest eats what the host offers him. But these angels did not eat. They did not eat because the angels are ṣumm, meaning they have no bodies with hollow interiors, as has been transmitted from the early generations (salaf). For this reason they have no need of eating or drinking. ﴿He felt a fear of them. They said, "Do not fear"﴾: they reassured him, saying, "Do not fear," when they saw on his face the sign of denial and fear. Every person knows the state of the heart of the one facing him: is he in joy? Is he in contentment? Is he afraid? Is he at peace? For this is a matter known by natural disposition, and it does not require great insight.

﴿And they gave him the good news of a learned boy﴾ (al-bushra) is the report of what delights, that is, they informed him of what would please him: a learned boy. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had reached great old age before he had a son, he and his wife. They gave him good news of this boy, and gave him good news that he would be learned, meaning he would be a man of knowledge, because God the Exalted made him one of the prophets, and the prophets are the most knowledgeable of creation about God, the Mighty and Majestic, His names, His attributes, His rulings and His acts. This learned boy is not the same as the forbearing boy, for the Qur'an states that Ibrahim was given good news of a learned boy in two verses of the Book of God, and of a forbearing boy in one verse. They are two boys: the forbearing boy is Isma'il, father of the Arabs, and the learned boy is Ishaq, father of the Children of Israel. This is why you find their stories differ.

Whoever claims that the forbearing boy is the learned boy has strayed far from the truth. Indeed, there is a clear text in Surat as-Saffat: when the Exalted related the story of the sacrificed son in Surat as-Saffat, He said after it: ﴿And We gave him good news of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [as-Saffat 112]. How, then, would He give good news of one who (...)? All of this shows that the saying that the forbearing boy is not the learned boy is correct.

﴿They gave him the good news of a learned boy﴾. This is good news, as you see, and it contained good news of two things, or if you wish, say three things:
Firstly: that a child would come to him who would reach the stage of being a boy.
Secondly: that this child would be a male, not a female, as indicated by His saying ﴿boy﴾.
Thirdly: that he would be ﴿learned﴾, that is, possessed of knowledge. Each of these good tidings is great; each one alone would suffice as good news.

The Exalted says: ﴿They gave him the good news of a learned boy (28). Then his wife came forward with an outcry﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 28, 29]. Who was this wife? She was Sarah, mother of Ishaq. ﴿Came forward﴾ when she heard the good news. ﴿With an outcry﴾: a cry or a shout. Was it out of joy, or regret and sorrow? The answer: she came ﴿with an outcry﴾ out of joy, because this good news came to her after old age had advanced upon her. She cried out, and it was as if she was saying, God knows best, "A boy! A boy!" That is, she struck her hand as one astonished, as people still do today when news reaches them... God is greatest, and she struck her face.

﴿She struck her face and said, "A barren old woman!"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 29]. ﴿An old woman﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, the implied meaning being: "I am a barren old woman." It was as though she was amazed that this good news of a learned boy should come to her after old age had advanced and she had become barren of children. But they explained to her the one sole cause by which this child would come into being, and said: ﴿Thus says your Lord﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 30], meaning: just as we have said and given you good news, so said God, the Mighty and Majestic.

Consider His saying ﴿your Lord﴾, where He attributed lordship here to this aged, barren, elderly woman, as a sign that this is from God's care for her, because attributing lordship to a particular person is a special lordship. Pay attention to the difference: general lordship belongs to everyone, for God is Lord of all things; special lordship belongs only to one who is particularly devoted to God. Let me recite to you this verse: ﴿They said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun"﴾ [al-A'raf 121, 122].

General lordship is ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾; special lordship is ﴿Lord of Musa and Harun﴾. Here they said to her, ﴿Your Lord says﴾, by way of special lordship which entails special care. ﴿They said, "Thus says your Lord. Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 30], the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise﴾: you may take ﴿He﴾ here as a subject (mubtada'), with ﴿the All-Wise﴾ as its predicate. Or you may take ﴿He﴾ as a pronoun of separation (damir fasl), with ﴿the All-Wise﴾ as the predicate. The choice is yours. That is, if you wish, say: ﴿the All-Wise﴾ is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾, and ﴿He﴾ is a pronoun of separation that has no grammatical position (la mahalla lahu min al-i'rab). Or if you wish, say: ﴿He﴾ is a subject, and ﴿the All-Wise﴾ is the predicate of ﴿He﴾, and the whole clause is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. Here ﴿the All-Wise﴾ is placed before ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, because the context here calls for placing wisdom before knowledge.

The wisdom here lies in two things, brothers. Firstly: the delay of the birth in relation to this woman. God did not delay her giving birth until she reached old age except for a wisdom. Another wisdom lies in her giving birth after she had despaired and believed herself barren. So there are two wisdoms here: a prior wisdom and a subsequent wisdom. Therefore the name ﴿the All-Wise﴾ is placed before the name ﴿the All-Knowing﴾. You observe that when God combines these two noble names, "the All-Knowing" and "the All-Wise," the Qur'an generally puts "the All-Knowing" first, but here it puts ﴿the All-Wise﴾ first, because the context requires it: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾.

Here I ask: what is the meaning of ﴿the All-Wise﴾? Most people think that the meaning of "al-Hakim" is one who possesses wisdom, and wisdom is placing a thing in its proper place. But in fact ﴿al-Hakim﴾ has two meanings: "wise" from wisdom (hikmah), and "judging" from judgement (hukm). God the Mighty and Majestic is "wise" in the sense of wisdom, and He is also the Judge (al-Hakam) among His servants, the one who rules over them and judges between them. God the Exalted has said in the noble Qur'an: ﴿And who is better in judgement than God, for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50]. ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾ [at-Tin 8], and this interrogation is for affirmation, meaning that God is the most judicious of judges. In Surat al-Ma'idah He said: ﴿And who is better in judgement than God?﴾, while in Surat at-Tin: ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾

Both are in their proper place. In Surat al-Ma'idah God mentioned: ﴿Whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, they are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44], ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45], ﴿the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah 47], and the verses continue until He said: ﴿Do they seek the judgement of the age of ignorance? And who is better in judgement than God for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50]. So the context there is a comparison between rulings, and He makes clear that God's judgement is the best of judgements. But in Surat at-Tin the context is one of authority and power, and God is the most judicious of judges, meaning that His judgement is binding and His authority complete, and no one can oppose His judgement, however mighty his strength.

Consider the Exalted's saying about 'Ad: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the land without right and said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾ [Fussilat 15], meaning: none is mightier than us in strength. God said: ﴿Did they not see that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15], and He punished them with the most subtle of things. With what did He punish them? With the wind, the subtle air that you do not feel as touch, though when it is strong, air pushes everything away, and it is stronger than water, as is well known. With this subtle air He destroyed those people who said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?" [Fussilat 15]; He destroyed them with it.

The sum of it is that God is the most judicious of judges: His judgement is binding, proceeding from power and authority. Furthermore, "the most judicious of judges" also includes excellence of judgement.

So ﴿al-Hakim﴾ in His saying ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾ includes two meanings: a meaning from judgement (hukm) and a meaning from wisdom (hikmah). Having finished with judgement: the judgement of God the Mighty and Majestic includes that He is the Judge over His servants, that He is the one who judges between His servants, and that His judgement is the best of judgements, and that He, the Exalted, is the most judicious of judges.

As for wisdom: to God belongs perfect wisdom, and none of the acts existing in the universe is more judicious than God's wisdom. If you believe this, O believer, then many matters that trouble many people become easy for you, including some of the legal rulings whose wisdom most people, or some of them, do not grasp. Do we say, when we do not grasp the wisdom, that there is no wisdom in it, or do we say that it has a wisdom, but our intellects are limited? The second. When we believe in this way, we become content with many legal matters whose wisdom is hidden from us. Do we grasp the wisdom in the prayers being five? No. Or that they are seventeen rak'ahs? No.

Many legal matters have wisdoms that a person does not grasp. But when you believe that God is All-Wise, you believe that this matter must have a wisdom that requires it.

Likewise in matters of predestination: God may send a punishment that encompasses the righteous and the wicked, and He may send punishment upon a people from whom you would never expect punishment to come. Do you say, "What is the wisdom?" Or do you say that God the Mighty and Majestic's decree in this must proceed from wisdom? Therefore I tell you: our duty, regarding what God has commanded in the laws and what He has decreed in destinies, is to submit with complete submission, and not to object to it with our intellects.

Listen to the Exalted's saying: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves; then they find in themselves no discomfort from what you have judged and submit in full acceptance﴾ [an-Nisa' 65]. This is the first condition; ﴿then they find in themselves no discomfort from what you have judged﴾ is the second; the third is ﴿and submit in full acceptance﴾.

God the Mighty and Majestic swore that no one can believe unless he meets these three conditions: that they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves.

The second: that they find no discomfort in their hearts, meaning: their hearts are not constricted by God's judgement.

Third: that they submit with full submission. He emphasized this with the verbal noun ﴿تَسْلِيمًا﴾, meaning complete submission, without a person being lax or slow in carrying out God's ruling. If you find in yourself a defect related to these three matters, then correct your faith. If you find that you would like judgment to be sought from other than Allah and His Messenger, correct your faith. If you find in your heart that you want nothing but the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, yet your chest is constricted by the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, while you tell yourself that you could never seek judgment from other than Allah and His Messenger, but your chest is constricted, then correct your faith. If your chest is not constricted, you do not desire judgment from other than Allah and His Messenger, and your heart is open to the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, but you are slow and lax, then your faith is deficient. Read the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight away, as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ [al-An'am 110].

Because they did not believe in it the first time and did not accept it from the first time, their hearts became fluctuating (may Allah protect us), and Allah left them in their transgression, wandering blindly. Therefore, O believer, you must hasten with complete submission to the divine decree of Allah the Exalted (...).

* * *

...And may Allah's peace and blessings be upon our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and upon his family and companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

We had reached the words of Allah, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 31].

However, I decided to speak about the etiquettes of greeting, since the angels said: ﴿Peace﴾, and Abraham said: ﴿Peace﴾. We mentioned earlier that Abraham's response was better than the angels' greeting, because Abraham's response was a nominal sentence, which indicates permanence and continuity, unlike the angels' greeting. Know that returning a greeting is obligatory, based on the words of Allah, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it or return it.﴾ [an-Nisa' 86]. He said ﴿when you are greeted﴾ and did not mention who greets us, so it includes any person who greets us. We greet them back, responding with something better than their greeting or its equal, as He said: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it or return it.﴾ [an-Nisa' 86]. He began with "better," because it is the more excellent, then ﴿or return it﴾, meaning return its equivalent. This includes the case where a Jew, a Christian, a Buddhist, or others greet us; we return the greeting. However, we do not initiate greeting with Jews and Christians, because the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade that.[[Narrated by Muslim (2167/13) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

Furthermore, the greeting is said this way: "As-salamu 'alaykum" (Peace be upon you). This is what is prescribed. As for "Ahlan wa sahlan," "Marhaban," "How are you?" and the like, these are not prescribed. What is prescribed is that you begin with the greeting first. Therefore, in the hadith of the Mi'raj (the Night Ascension), when the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by the prophets and greeted them, he said: "He returned the greeting and said: 'Welcome, righteous Prophet.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (349) and Muslim (163/263) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]] So begin first by saying: "As-salamu 'alaykum." The reply should be like it or better: "Wa 'alaykumu as-salam," or "'Alaykum as-salam," or "'Alaykum as-salam wa rahmatullah," or "'Alaykum as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." All of this is prescribed. We see many people, when greeted, say: "Ahlan wa sahlan," or say "Marhaban, Abu so-and-so." This does not suffice. Even if he said, "Ahlan wa sahlan" for the rest of his life, it would not suffice, because Allah says: ﴿Greet with better than it or return it.﴾ [an-Nisa' 86]. It is well known that the one who says "as-salamu 'alayka" is invoking peace upon you from every deficiency, every affliction, and every sickness of the heart or body. It is not enough to say "Marhaban" and "Ahlan"; you must say "'Alayka as-salam" or "Wa 'alaykumu as-salam." If you add "wa rahmatullah wa barakatuh," it is better.

Second: who is required to greet first? The Sunnah (the recommended practice of the Prophet (ﷺ)) has explained this: "The young should greet the elderly,"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6231) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] because the elderly person's right is greater than the young person's right over the elderly. So the young person begins the greeting to the elderly. But if it is assumed that he does not greet, should the elderly person forgo the greeting because the right is his, or greet so that the Sunnah is not lost? The answer: he should greet, so that the Sunnah is not lost. For a person to say, "I am the one with the right; why did he not greet me?" is a mistake. It is true that you have the right, and that it is prescribed for him to greet you, but if he does not do so, then you greet. Likewise, "the one walking greets the one sitting," even if the sitting one is younger. If a person passes by someone seated, he should greet him, even if he is younger in age or status. It was part of the guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he would greet children when he passed by them.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6247) and Muslim (2168/14) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] In this there is great benefit:

Among them: humility, for a person lowers himself when he greets one who is beneath him.

Among them: mercy, for your greeting of the young is a form of mercy, and the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that the merciful are shown mercy by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4941) and al-Tirmidhi (1924) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As.]]

Among them: accustoming these children to greeting; that is, the child learns that the emblem of the Muslims is that they greet one another, and he takes from this a manner and character that benefits him in his youth and in his old age.

Third: the many greet the few, or the few greet the many: which of them has the greater right? The few, like the young with the elderly, greets the many. That is, when a group of five or six meet, who greets? The five greet the six, because the six have something more, and this extra has a right; the one who is more has a right. So the few greet the many. If they do not do so, then the many should greet the few, so that the Sunnah is not lost between them. Likewise, the rider and the walker: if two men meet, one walking and the other riding in his car or on his camel, who greets? The rider greets the walker, because the rider is higher, so he greets the walker, for the Sunnah came with this. Does the one ascending greet the one descending, or the one descending greet the one ascending? The one ascending greets the one descending. That is, if two people meet on a staircase, the one ascending is the one who greets the one descending. If the one who should initiate does not, then the second should initiate. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is not lawful for a Muslim to shun his brother for more than three days; when they meet, one turns away and the other turns away, and the better of them is the one who initiates the greeting."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6077) and Muslim (2560/25) from the hadith of Abu Ayyub.]] He said: "the better of them," which indicates that whoever initiates the greeting to another is better. This is so, because when you greet, you gain ten good deeds. Then, when your companion returns it, he gains ten good deeds. What is the cause that made him gain ten good deeds? The initiating cause. Had you not greeted, he would not have returned it. So you are the means for this one doing a righteous deed, and you have a share of its reward. For this reason the scholars said: initiating the greeting is a Sunnah, and returning it is obligatory. Then they raised a difficulty, saying: which is more excellent, initiating the greeting or returning it? Initiating the greeting is more excellent. Then they raised a difficulty, saying: how can the Sunnah be more excellent than the obligatory? The established legal principle is that the obligatory is more excellent, as Allah the Exalted said in the hadith qudsi (a hadith in which God speaks in the first person): "My servant draws near to Me with nothing more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6502) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

They answered this, saying: the answer to this difficulty is that this obligation was built upon the Sunnah. So the Sunnah upon which the obligation was built becomes, for the one who performs it, the reward of his specific act together with the reward of the obligatory reply.

Likewise, the greeting should be audible. Some people meet you and greet you, but you are unsure whether they greeted or not, because they did not raise their voice. This is an error. Raise your voice in a manner that shows you are pleased with this brother who met you, or whom you greeted, not with a jarring voice, nor with a voice so low that it cannot be heard. On the contrary, some people greet with a jarring voice, while the religion is a middle path between extremism and negligence. So we say: greet with a greeting that your brother can hear, and do so with courtesy and respect.

Among the etiquettes of greeting also: the one greeting should have a cheerful face and an open chest. It is well known that you should meet your brother with a radiant face.[[Narrated by Muslim (2626/144) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]] Radiance of face, openness of the chest, and a smile toward your brother are undoubtedly among the matters that are sought, because they bring joy to your brothers. Bringing joy to your brothers is among the recommended matters for which you are rewarded, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every act of kindness is charity."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6021) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah, and Muslim (1005/52) from the hadith of Huzayfah.]] Every act of kindness is charity.

If a greeting reaches you through a messenger, and the one who carries it is a person who says, "So-and-so sends you greetings," then say: "'Alayka wa 'alayhi as-salam" (Upon you and upon him be peace). If you wish, you may say: "'Alayhi as-salam," meaning upon the one who sent it.

As for a greeting conveyed in writing: that is, a person writes you a letter and says: "As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." If you want to reply by letter, respond to him in your reply. For example, a person wrote you a letter and said, "As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." When replying, you write: "J" (meaning "jawab," answer), "Wa 'alaykumu as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. I have read your letter and understood what is in it, and the answer is such and such." Most people now do not pay attention to this. You find them writing the reply and beginning with "As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah." This is good, but the one who greeted you wants a reply. Say: "J," meaning the answer: "Wa 'alaykumu as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Your letter reached me, or I read your letter and understood what is in it. This is the answer," and you answer what he asked. So when the greeting is written, its reply is in writing.

I do not say it is obligatory, because your friend will not hear it, but it is a recommended act. If a man invokes blessings for you in your absence, then you invoke blessings for him in his absence.

Here the discussion of greeting ends.

We have reached the words of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?" (31) They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a people of criminals."﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 31, 32].

The essential point is that they all agree on killing him, and there is no doubt that killing him is the wisdom; for when this indecency spreads among men, men become like women, and disgrace, humiliation and shame appear on the face of the one who is done to, which he does not forget until he dies.

When these people are executed, and they are in reality a corrupt germ that corrupts the person, that is precisely the benefit.

No one who sees two males walking in the market can object to their being together; but fornication can be guarded against: if you see a man with a woman, you disapprove of him, or accuse him, or speak with him. Therefore the execution of the sodomite is most suited to wisdom and also to mercy. It is mercy to whom? Mercy to the doers: that is, the one who sodomizes and the one who is sodomized, so that they do not remain throughout their lives accumulating sin and increasing their punishment; and mercy to society, the punishment being a deterrent, so that society is not corrupted. ﴿To send down upon them stones of clay (33) marked by your Lord for the transgressors﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 33, 34]. ﴿Stones of clay﴾, but not clay that crumbles; rather hard, great clay, which, when such a stone strikes a person and hits him on the head, comes out from his posterior, neither bone nor flesh can repel it, because of its strength, hardness and solidity, we seek refuge in Allah; and it is marked.

The meaning of ﴿marked﴾ is: designated with Allah; i.e., it bears a sign; because everything with Allah is according to a measure. Do not think that the matters Allah, Mighty and Majestic, decrees come by mere chance; rather they are by measure, even the distances between the stars now and the variation in their size and brightness are by measure; it did not come about by accident or coincidence; everything is decreed precisely, down to the hair's breadth or finer. Everything with Allah is by a measure, without fail. These stones are marked with Allah. The answer: the second, because this is more precise: this stone is for so-and-so, this stone is for so-and-so.

﴿Marked by your Lord for the transgressors﴾, i.e., for those who exceed their limits. And there is no doubt that sodomy is transgressing the bound and extravagance, we seek refuge in Allah.

"We brought them out" means: We commanded them with a decree of destiny (amran qadariyyan), and they went out. Allah the Exalted said to Lot: ﴿So travel with your family in a part of the night, and let not any of you look back, except your wife﴾ [Hud 81].

﴿We brought out those who were in it of the believers﴾. Who were they? Lot and his family, except his wife; for this reason He said: ﴿And We found not in it any but one house of the Muslims﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 36].

One house. A whole town, whose prophet called them to the Oneness of Allah and to abandoning this vile sin, and no one followed him, not even his own household fully believed; among them were those who did not believe in Lot. So pay attention, my brother, pay attention, my brother the caller to Islam: do not despair when you call and only ten out of a hundred respond to you. This is a blessing. The messengers, peace be upon them, remain among their peoples for many ages, and only a few follow them. Lot, peace be upon him: who followed him from the town? No one. Who followed him from his family? Some of his family followed him, and some of them stayed behind from his call; for this reason He said: ﴿And We found not in it any but one house of the Muslims﴾.

Here a person asks himself: how did He say: ﴿We brought out those who were in it of the believers (35) And We found not in it any but one house of the Muslims﴾? Are the "Muslims" here the same as the "believers" in the verse before it?

Some scholars held that this is so, and said: in this there is evidence that faith (iman) and Islam are one thing.

Others held that there is a difference, and said: as for the believers, they were saved; and as for the house, it is a house of Islam, because the outward appearance of this house, Lot's house, was that it was an Islamic house. Even his wife did not openly display disbelief; she displayed that she was a Muslim. For this reason Allah the Exalted said in Surat at-Tahrim: ﴿Allah presents an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. The meaning of ﴿they betrayed them﴾ is not betrayal by immorality, but betrayal by disbelief, yet it was hidden disbelief, and it is a betrayal of the kind of hypocrisy. For this reason a society in which there are hypocrites is called a Muslim society, even if hypocrites are in it, because its outward appearance is Islamic.

So we say: ﴿And We found not in it any but one house of the Muslims﴾; He said "of the Muslims" only because his wife was not a believer, but she was a Muslim.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 51, verse 37:

﴿So We found in it no household other than the submitters (Muslims) (36). And We left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 36, 37]

﴿We left in it a sign﴾ means: an indication. So what is the sign? Is it a sensory (physical) sign, a meaningful (moral or spiritual) sign, or two signs, one meaningful and one sensory?

I will tell you a useful principle in tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis): if a verse can bear more than one meaning, with no preference for one over the other and no contradiction between them, then it must be understood as referring to both meanings together. We say that this verse is both sensory and meaningful. The sensory sign is what is seen from the place of their town, which is called the Lake of Lot (Bahr Lut). This was the site of the town, and everyone who passes by it sees and observes it, as God Most High said: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning (137), and at night. Will you not then use your reason?﴾ [As-Saffat: 137, 138]

The meaningful sign: everyone who reads their story in all the noble surahs where it appears takes heed, is admonished, and fears (God). This is the meaningful sign. But who benefits from these signs? Those who fear the painful punishment, ﴿for those who fear the painful punishment﴾. As for the deniers whose hearts have hardened, they will not benefit from the signs. God Most High said: ﴿But signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus: 101]. We ask God to make us and you among those who benefit from the signs. The discussion of the story of Abraham and Lot, peace be upon them, has ended (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 51, verse 38–39:

We have reached the words of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And in Musa (Moses) [there is a sign] when We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority. But he turned away with his supporters and said, "A magician or a madman."﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 38, 39]. The meaning: in Musa there are signs from the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, when Allah Most High sent him to Pharaoh. "Pharaoh" is a generic name (ʿalam jins) for everyone who ruled Egypt, and he was a disbeliever. Musa is the son of ʿImran, the most excellent of the prophets of the Children of Israel, and he holds the third rank in excellence among the Ulul-ʿAzm (the five prophets of firm resolve), for the most excellent of them is Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, then Ibrahim (Abraham), then Musa, then Nuh (Noah), and ʿIsa (Jesus).

Allah sent him ﴿with clear authority﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 38], i.e., with a proof that is clear in itself and makes other things clear. The signs that the prophets brought are clear and evident to everyone who is just and fair, and they also make clear the truthfulness of what the messengers brought. For this reason, know that whenever the word "mubin" (clear) appears in the Qur'an, it means: clear in itself and making clear for others, unless the context shows that the intended meaning is only "clear in itself."

﴿When We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority﴾. Among the great signs that Musa brought was the staff, the staff of Musa, which he used to lean upon when needed, and with which he would knock down leaves from trees for his sheep when they grazed, and it had other uses as well, as he himself said, peace be upon him, when Allah asked him: ﴿"What is that in your right hand, O Musa?" He said, "It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I beat down [leaves] with it for my sheep, and I have in it other uses."﴾ [Ta-Ha 17, 18]. It was a sign in that when he placed it on the ground it became a clearly visible serpent (thuʿban mubin), i.e., a great snake that frightened whoever saw it. For this reason Musa, peace be upon him, was terrified of it when he threw it and fled, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, called out to him: ﴿"Fear not"﴾ [an-Naml 10].

Among them: he would put his hand into his pocket (jayb), and it would come out white at once, white but without harm (suʾ), i.e., without defect. That is, it was not white from leprosy (baras); rather, it was white in a way that differed from the color of his skin, immediately, as a real fact and not as an illusion.

Allah Most High said in Surat al-Isra: ﴿And We gave Musa nine clear signs﴾ [al-Isra 101]. The point is that he came to Pharaoh with clear authority and a decisive, far-reaching proof, but he, may Allah protect us, ﴿turned away with his supporters﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 39], i.e., with his strength, his authority and his army. He turned away from Musa out of arrogance, denial, injustice and aggression. Allah Most High said: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and haughtiness﴾ [an-Naml 14].

﴿So he turned away with his supporters and said, "A magician or a madman"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 39]. The meaning: he accused Musa, peace be upon him, of being a magician, because he brought signs resembling what magicians do: a staff of wood that is placed on the ground and becomes a clearly visible serpent, and a hand that enters the pocket and comes out white at once. This resembles magic.

﴿Or a madman﴾: the meaning is that he said he is mad. This was because he claimed that Allah alone is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, that He is the Lord and the God; for they did not recognize any god except whom? Except Pharaoh. So when a person comes saying, "He is Allah, Lord of the worlds, and Pharaoh is neither a god nor a lord," they call him mad. This is a madman who has gone beyond what we know, beyond what is familiar.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We seized him and his hosts, and cast them into the sea﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 40]. That is: We threw them into it. Al-yamm is the sea, and the sea in which Pharaoh was destroyed is the Red Sea, which lies between Asia and Africa. The reason was that Pharaoh gathered his soldiers and mustered them, intending to destroy Musa and his people. Musa and his people left Egypt heading east, but the sea stood between them and their goal. When they reached the sea, the sea was before them and Pharaoh and his people were behind them. They said to Musa: ﴿Indeed, we are overtaken﴾ [ash-Shu'ara 61]; meaning: we are lost, for Pharaoh is behind us and the sea is in front of us, so how is deliverance to be found? He said: ﴿No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [ash-Shu'ara 62]. This is a special companionship (ma'iyya khassa) which entails victory and support.

His saying ﴿He will guide me﴾ rather than "He will guide me soon" (sawfa yahdini): he said ﴿sayahdini﴾, indicating the nearness of this confinement and that it would soon pass away, and this is what occurred. Allah the Exalted inspired him to strike the sea with his staff, so he struck it and it split into twelve paths immediately, and it dried up immediately, and became fit to walk upon at once, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿So strike for them a dry path through the sea, not fearing being overtaken, nor being afraid﴾ [Ta-Ha 77].

Thus Musa and his people crossed through these great paths, with the water between them like mountains. When they had finished, emerging on the far side, Pharaoh was on their trail, and when they had completed their crossing, the Mighty and Majestic, by His power and authority, commanded the sea to return to what it had been, so it closed over Pharaoh and his people, and they perished to the last one, and all praise is due to Allah. For this reason He said: ﴿So We cast them into the sea, and he was blameworthy﴾, that is: Pharaoh was one who did what deserved blame, and there is no doubt that his rejection of the divine message and his claim to be the Lord were blameworthy.

And His saying ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas 38], and what is similar to such words, are undoubtedly words for which he is blamed, because the truth had become clear to him, but he was obstinate and refused to submit to the truth. As Musa said to him: ﴿Indeed you have known﴾, meaning: O Pharaoh, ﴿that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights; and indeed I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed﴾ [al-Isra' 102] (...).

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And in 'Ad, when We sent upon them the barren wind﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 41]. That is: And in 'Ad there are signs, ﴿when We sent upon them the barren wind﴾. 'Ad were in the south of the Arabian Peninsula, and they were a people of great strength, to the extent that they said: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ So Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength? Yet they were rejecting Our signs﴾ [Fussilat 15]. Then drought and famine struck them, and they began to await rain, so Allah sent upon them a great and violent wind.

﴿When they saw it as a cloud coming towards their valleys, they said: "This is a cloud that will bring us rain."﴾ Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, it is that which you were seeking to hasten: a wind wherein is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf 24]. Allah sent upon them this barren wind, which has no fruit and carries no water, like the barren woman who does not bear children. This too is a great wind that carries no cloud and no rain. This barren wind is the western wind, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was helped by the eastern wind (as-Saba), and 'Ad were destroyed by the western wind (ad-Dabur)" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1035) and Muslim (900/17), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas]. That is, by the western wind.

Allah sent upon them this barren wind ﴿that leaves nothing it comes upon without making it like that which is crumbled to dust﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 42]. Everything it passes over it makes ﴿like that which is crumbled﴾, dry and ruined. Indeed, it would lift a man—may Allah protect us—up into the air, then hurl him back down to the earth, and they became ﴿as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Haqqah 7], ﴿as if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾ [al-Qamar 20]. They were destroyed to the last one of them.

So reflect on this verse: a stubborn, powerful, mighty people were destroyed by this gentle wind, whose body you cannot see; you only feel it without seeing anything, yet by the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, it brought them to their end. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿that leaves nothing it comes upon without making it like that which is crumbled to dust﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 42]. In this there is a sign from the signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: Allah sent this wind upon them and it destroyed them to the last one, so there are signs in them: ﴿that leaves nothing it comes upon without making it like that which is crumbled to dust﴾.﴿

And in Thamud [too], when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a time." (51:43)

Thamud were the people to whom Allah sent His Prophet Salih, peace be upon him. He admonished them and reminded them, and He gave them a sign: the she-camel, which Allah honoured by attributing her to Himself, as He, blessed and exalted is He, says: ﴿So the Messenger of Allah said to them, "[Beware of] the she-camel of Allah and her drink."﴾ (91:13). That is, "Beware of the she-camel of Allah, lest you harm her or deny her."

This camel had a share of water, drinking from the well that is called "the well of the she-camel," and they had ﴿a share of water on a known day﴾ (26:155) which they would drink. So the camel drank one day and they drank one day. It is reported that whenever anyone came to draw water from this well on the day she drank from it, he would receive in exchange for her share some of her milk equal to the amount she had drunk. Allah knows best whether this was the actual reality or whether it differed. But in any case, this camel was undoubtedly not like the other camels, for she was a sign from the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Yet they denied and refused, and Salih, peace be upon him, threatened them that they would enjoy themselves in their homes for three days. But they persisted in their disbelief and denial. For this reason He said: ﴿And in Thamud [too], when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a time."﴾

Their dwellings are well known today; they exist in a place called al-Hijr, which is now called the dwellings of Thamud. The Prophet ﷺ passed by them on his way to Tabuk, but when he passed by these dwellings he hastened, covered his head, and forbade his Ummah to enter these places of the punished except while weeping. He said: "If you are not weeping, then do not enter them, lest there befall you what befell them." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2980/38), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar.]

His saying "lest there befall you what befell them" does not necessarily mean that what is intended is the sensory punishment that befell them. It may be that what is intended is both the sensory punishment that befell them and what befell them of aversion and disbelief. So if someone were to say: "There are people who go to these places, not weeping, and nothing has befallen them," 

We say: The answer to this is in two respects:

First: The Messenger ﷺ did not affirm that they would certainly be afflicted with this; rather he said: "out of fear" or "lest" they be afflicted with what afflicted those.

Second: We say: it is not necessarily the case that what is meant is that they will be seized with the same visible sensory punishment that those received, namely the quaking and the cry that destroyed them all to the last one. What may be meant is the sickness of the heart, which is arrogance, aversion, and rejection of the truth.

﴿When it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a time."﴾ This "time" was three days, the end of three days. ﴿But they defied the command of their Lord﴾ (51:44), and did not turn back from their error. ﴿So the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on﴾. The thunderbolt which was their destruction was a quaking and a cry. ﴿While they were looking on﴾: that is, some of them were looking at others, collapsing and falling down dead.
